title: The bitter personal feud that could imperil a key Senate race for Democrats
excerpt: Mike Rogers, a Republican from Michigan and US Senate candidate, and Rep
body: Mike Rogers, a Republican from Michigan and US Senate candidate, and Rep

Haley Stevens (D-MI), speak to members of the media following a service at Perfecting Church in Detroit, Michigan, on November 1, 2026. | Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images Democrats in Michigan spent the weekend before Election Day angrily relitigating their Senate primary from months earlier after a defeated candidate, Rep
Haley Stevens, took back her endorsement of Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed — and backed the Republican instead
Haley Stevens had previously endorsed her primary rival, Abdul El-Sayed, in his general election contest against Republican Mike Rogers, but she switched over to Rogers’s camp on Sunday
Stevens has cited comments Abdul El-Sayed made about Israel, and especially an ad from a PAC supporting El-Sayed that she viewed as antisemitic, in explaining her shift
Democrats, including many longtime Stevens supporters and staffers, near-unanimously denounced her for endorsing Rogers, often in harsh personal terms
The hope among Democrats is that this is essentially a personal feud and it won’t change many voters’ minds

On the surface, the fight gets to the heart of issues that have divided Democrats all year — between the party’s populist left-wing faction and its politically cautious centrists, and between vocal supporters and harsh critics of Israel — and that Republicans have hoped to ride to victory in Michigan an otherwise difficult election year.  But it also is the culmination of a complicated and ongoing personal feud between the candidates — leading Democrats to hope that the damage might be contained, and that it was not representative of a broader shift within the electorate they’ve spent months working to consolidate.  How Sunday’s shock endorsement came about Initially, Stevens seemed to be enthusiastically on board with the party’s effort to bring Democrats together.  Shortly after Stevens narrowly lost the hard-fought Michigan Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, she endorsed El-Sayed and pledged her support in the general election
And though Stevens had begun to publicly criticize El-Sayed more in recent weeks, she reiterated in a CNN interview Wednesday that she’d vote for him

Multiple reports indicated she’d said the same to prominent Democrats as well, some as recently as Saturday.  But just two days before Election Day, Stevens stunningly reversed course — and endorsed El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep
The turnabout came after a days-long, tense back-and-forth between Stevens and El-Sayed, in which influential Democratic Reps
James Clyburn of South Carolina and Debbie Dingell of Michigan tried to negotiate an agreement for the former rivals to appear together at a unity event before the election
Despite Stevens’s earlier endorsement, however, she had soured on El-Sayed in recent weeks because of the chief topic that divided them back during the primary: Israel

In particular, Stevens wanted El-Sayed to denounce an advertisement aired by a PAC backing him that she viewed as antisemitic, rather than just disavow any association with the ad, as he had done initially.  On Friday morning, Stevens posted an odd statement praising El-Sayed’s “expected condemnation” of the ad in advance of their joint campaign appearance
Then, by the end of the day Friday, El-Sayed’s campaign was letting it be known that the event was off, and that Stevens should stay away to avoid causing a distraction

And Sunday, soon after appearing with Rogers at a Detroit church where she praised his record helping Black communities, Stevens released a video endorsing Rogers, mentioning how El-Sayed told her to “stay away” from his campaign

She added, “Who we are as Michiganders is not hate, and is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now.” Her endorsement was a coup for Rogers and his allies, who have been working to convince habitual Democratic voters — and Black and Jewish Michiganders, in particular — to treat El-Sayed as an extremist they should consider beyond the pale
And while polling is hardly any guarantee of the outcome, surveys have shown El-Sayed narrowly but consistently leading Rogers, suggesting this strategy was not getting the job done for Republicans

Yet it was also notable how quickly and vociferously Democrats across the board, including some of Stevens’s closest allies, spoke up to denounce what she had done.  More than half of Stevens’s congressional staff resigned in protest of her endorsement of Rogers
Michigan’s Democratic Party chair even declared that Stevens was no longer a member of the party and would not be permitted to rejoin it

And Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who had strongly favored Stevens in the primary, called her actions “a despicable betrayal” and stressed that the party was “united in our support” for El-Sayed.  Some pointed fingers at Stevens’s fiancé Jason Turkish, an attorney and Democratic donor who endorsed Rogers days earlier, and did a media tour predicting Stevens would soon do the same
So the question is whether this last-minute drama exposes a real fissure inside the party — or whether this mess is more a tension of the specific personalities of the people involved

Why did Stevens turn against El-Sayed? At the heart of Stevens’s public criticism of El-Sayed were disputes over how to handle Israel, and where the line stood between criticism and antisemitism, a debate that has at times badly split Democrats this cycle
Stevens, first elected to Congress in 2018, has been a longtime champion of Israel
In 2022, when she was redistricted into the same district as Rep

Andy Levin — a Jewish Democrat who’d been sharply critical of the Netanyahu government — Stevens beat him in the primary, backed by $4 million in spending from AIPAC. (I interviewed Levin about that contest earlier this year.) But this year, in Michigan’s Senate primary, she faced El-Sayed — a very vocal critic of Israel and of the Democratic establishment’s backing of the Gaza war
And as the two sparred over Israel policy, AIPAC once again backed Stevens – this time, spending more than $30 million on the primary, the group’s biggest-ever investment in a single election

Stevens ended up losing the August primary by a margin of less than 1 percentage point; soon afterward she endorsed El-Sayed and hugged him at a unity breakfast. “It’s a big-tent party,” she said then

She said it was time to focus on beating Mike Rogers and the GOP, and that “the time for all this negative, nasty, the disunity stuff — it’s over.” Yet they did not campaign together after that, and an account by CNN’s Edward-Isaac Dovere of the continuing tensions between them last week seemed to put most of that on the El-Sayed campaign; Dovere’s sources portrayed El-Sayed as uninterested in cultivating the relationship.  Then, Stevens told the New York Times , her doubts had been reignited because of an October 8 debate in which El-Sayed repeatedly refused to answer a moderator’s question about whether he thought Israel or Iran was a greater threat to the United States. (El-Sayed called it a “ridiculous hypothetical” and said both were “kind of dangerous,” with “one at risk of attacking us, one getting us into wars we have no business fighting.”) After that, on October 23, the pro-El-Sayed PAC released its controversial ad , in which people say grocery prices were high because too much government money is being spent helping Israel with “killing Palestinians” and funding Israelis’ universal healthcare

The ad closed by saying Mike Rogers was for “they/them” (over pictures of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right allies), while “Abdul El-Sayed is for you.” The ad — put out by Cenk Uygur, a left-wing commentator who is the uncle of streamer Hasan Piker — was reused from 2024 and had little money behind it
But it went viral online, and critics called it antisemitic.  The ad became a major sticking point in Stevens’s negotiations with the El-Sayed team

Turkish, her fiancé, publicly denounced it as antisemitic, blaming El-Sayed for putting “Jews at risk.” And though El-Sayed’s spokesperson had said the ad didn’t speak for their campaign, Stevens wanted a more unambiguous condemnation.  So on Friday morning, Stevens posted her unusual statement promising to campaign with El-Sayed on Sunday and praising his “expected” condemnation of the ad. “A unifying moment has arrived, our democratic nominee for U.S Senate disavows the Rebellion PAC ad made by Hasan Piker’s uncle that claims Jews are responsible for America’s economic woes
We have learned from party leaders and emissaries, as reported in the news media that he has,” Stevens posted on X

This was widely taken as an ultimatum to El-Sayed, and he decided not to play ball; word leaked out that his campaign did not want Stevens at any of their events anymore. “Our campaign is and always has been focused on addressing the most critical challenges Michiganders are facing,” he posted . “Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on litigating a primary that ended three months ago.” At a campaign event Saturday, El-Sayed was asked about the ad, and said : “That ad was not made by me, and I do not agree with the contents of that ad.” He also called it “not really of relevance to Michigan voters.” Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers came the following day.  And after that, came the backlash from Stevens’s fellow Democrats

The Democratic response to Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers Within hours, Stevens was effectively ostracized from the party, with even her own top aides abandoning her.  Stevens’s chief of staff Justin German said in a statement that he had served with her for eight years, and that he was “shocked and heartbroken” by her endorsement of Rogers, adding: “As of this morning, many members of our team have resigned, including myself.” Neera Tanden, the longtime Democratic aide and Center for American Progress president who had been arguably Stevens’s most aggressive online defender during the primary, wrote that standing with Rogers was “a betrayal of everything Haley Stevens has fought for her entire career” and “a betrayal of all of her supporters that believed in her.” Former Rep
Susan Wild (D-PA) posted about her years-long friendship with Stevens — they were roommates, and Wild said her adult children text with Stevens

She said she was “shocked” by Stevens’s “appalling” endorsement of Rogers. “So many people in the Democratic Party have shown so much support to Haley over the years, and she has betrayed them all.” Wild continued: “If this is because of her new relationship (about which many of us were so happy for her after she lost the primary), all I can say is that any woman who abandons her friends when a new guy comes along is no friend at all.” Several critics, including Schumer, implicitly questioned why Stevens was so willing to overlook Rogers’s lack of condemnation of the Islamophobia that Trump and Republicans have aimed at El-Sayed. (Trump has repeatedly called El-Sayed a “ jihadist ,” a phrase he repeated to reporters in response to the Stevens news on Sunday.) “We Democrats,” Schumer said , are “united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans.” The Stevens fight could matter beyond Michigan The loud condemnations from Democrats spoke to the importance of the race, but also to the complex and high-stakes role it plays in various factional fights within the party.  Moderate Democrats, who spent Sunday racing to distance themselves from Stevens, worried her endorsement was a potential cudgel that could be used to portray future moderate candidates as either unreliable pseudo-Republicans or too closely tied to pro-Israel groups.  But it also threatened to empower the left in different ways, even as it complicated El-Sayed’s closing message

El-Sayed is one of the first candidates from the Bernie Sanders wing of the party to be nominated in a competitive statewide race, and his performance — even the margin of victory, should he win — is under heavy scrutiny by moderates and progressives looking for evidence that their favored candidates are stronger electoral performers

As some commentators noted, an El-Sayed loss or underperformance now might be viewed through a different lens after Stevens’s switch. “Ironically if El-Sayed loses it will now be much harder to blame his progressivism since people can just blame Haley Stevens instead,” elections analyst Nate Silver said on X . “I’m not saying that’s right, I’m not saying that’s wrong, but that’s how the intraparty D debate is likely to go.”

title: Haley Stevens Is Sending the Wrong Message
excerpt: ET on November 1, 2026 Haley Stevens nearly won the Democratic nomination for Senate in Michigan in August, then immediately endorsed the winner, Abdul El-Sayed
body: ET on November 1, 2026 Haley Stevens nearly won the Democratic nomination for Senate in Michigan in August, then immediately endorsed the winner, Abdul El-Sayed
She has spent the months since then vacillating, expressing doubts about his campaign while maintaining her support
But last week, her fiancé said that he intends to vote for El-Sayed’s opponent, Mike Rogers, and now she has followed, endorsing the Republican just two days before the election
Stevens’s dramatic reversal met with immediate cries of opportunism or political stupidity
But Stevens seems instead to be following through on a principled objection to El-Sayed’s rhetoric and associations that threaten the state’s Jewish population
The trouble is that her application of those principles is misguided, undermining the values she claims to uphold
Before this weekend, Stevens could credibly accuse El-Sayed of overlooking the bigotry of his allies out of political expedience
I grew up in West Bloomfield, Michigan, a heavily Jewish suburb of Detroit, and have many friends and family who still live in the state
Every Jewish Michigander I know has serious concerns about El-Sayed

Their issue is not only that he refuses to accept Israel’s right to exist; it’s that he elevated anti-Zionism into the centerpiece of his primary campaign, treating the Israel lobby as the singular force lying behind every economic and political problem afflicting America
During the campaign, he has energized an activist cohort whose rhetoric habitually goes beyond mere criticism of Israel, or even anti-Zionism, and extends into conspiratorial anti-Semitism
He campaigned with Amir Makled , a candidate for University of Michigan’s Board of Regents who had reposted some of Candace Owens’s anti-Semitic tweets
More notorious, he attached himself to Hasan Piker, a Marxist-Leninist who has repeatedly employed anti-Semitic rhetoric

When a network of anti-Israel protestors was charged with plotting to intimidate local Jews, El-Sayed questioned the indictment, telling reporters, “It’s a lot more about what you’re advocating for that gets you indicted or not indicted, rather than what you did.” El-Sayed has made some concessions to the Jewish community
He apologized for his response to a terrorist attack on a Jewish nursery school (“hurt people hurt people”), which he acknowledged minimized the pain felt by the attack’s targets
But for the most part he has tried to strike a very careful balance, assuaging liberal Jews without alienating any elements of his anti-Zionist base
After the left-wing media personality Cenk Uygur released an advertisement blaming Israel for the cost of groceries, Stevens demanded he renounce it
El-Sayed took days to reply, finally stating, “I do not agree with the contents of that ad,” without describing it as offensive

As the American left has grown more fixated on Gaza, it is becoming more common for progressive organizations and cultures to treat Zionism in any form—including liberal Zionism that harshly criticizes Israel’s government—as a racist ideology, and to ostracize anybody who refuses to renounce it
American Jews rationally fear that El-Sayed is not only willing but eager to import this norm into the Democratic Party, functionally excluding the overwhelming majority of the Jewish population
Jewish Democrats who have a defter touch than Stevens have tried to work through their reservations, with little success

Josh Whinston, a rabbi in Ann Arbor, wrote an op-ed in the Detroit Free Press conveying his fears about El-Sayed’s rhetoric and political alliances, and El-Sayed’s apparent lack of interest in allaying them
Whinston wrote that he has “said, again and again, that there is a way forward together that does not ask him to abandon his values

He has not yet responded.” Jordan Acker, a Michigan regent whose home was vandalized in the middle of the night by anti-Israel activists, told The New Yorker , “My top issue is the safety of my children, and nothing I’ve heard from the El-Sayed campaign suggests they take that seriously at all.” Both Whinston and Acker, despite their reservations about El-Sayed, have ruled out endorsing Rogers
Stevens did too , before abruptly reversing course after El-Sayed disinvited her from a preelection unity rally

This decision by El-Sayed, which undercuts the most essential function of a unity rally, is characteristic of his preference for refusing to break ranks with his most left-wing, fanatically anti-Zionist supporters
Whether or not you agree with El-Sayed’s ethic—I do not—one must acknowledge that he is willing to follow it even at some risk to his chances of winning
In this way, El-Sayed, like Stevens, appears to care more about putting his own stamp on the Democratic Party than defeating the Republicans
The trouble is that her principled opposition to religious and ethnic intolerance does not extend to Muslim and Arab communities

During the same period of time that El-Sayed has been winking at a political movement inflected with anti-Semitism, he has been targeted by a political message that is not merely inflected with racism but saturated with it

Donald Trump has made hysterical attacks on El-Sayed, such as “I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” and accused him of planning to impose Sharia law, among other wild charges
Rather than use his first name, he has sneeringly called El-Sayed “Muhammed,” as if to erase all doubt that his objection is not to any position El-Sayed has taken but to his religion
Rogers has not repudiated any of this rhetoric
Instead, he has charged El-Sayed with refusing to condemn the Muslim Brotherhood, even after El-Sayed did precisely that
Perhaps the party of Trump is so deeply corrupted by racism that hoping a Republican would renounce it is absurd, like asking a shark to apologize for mauling a swimmer
But Stevens is not a Republican or a Trump supporter
And she has thrown herself behind Rogers without making any demands of him
Tolerance cannot be the ethical rationale for doing so
It’s impossible to construct any standard of behavior toward religious minorities that El-Sayed fails but Rogers passes
And so, whatever message Stevens imagines she is conveying, it is not what is coming across

title: Trump Searches for a Fall Guy to Blame for Iran
excerpt: ET on November 1, 2026 P resident Trump is deciding whether a resumption of strikes in Iran will finally deliver the victory he has already claimed he’s achieve
body: ET on November 1, 2026 P resident Trump is deciding whether a resumption of strikes in Iran will finally deliver the victory he has already claimed he’s achieved

He also has two other questions to answer closer to home: Who gets the blame for a war his advisers assured him would end well before the midterms? And can he trust those same advisers when they tell him that the new plan will succeed where previous plans have failed? For weeks, Trump has been contemplating a renewal of hostilities aimed at forcing Iran to negotiate, and advisers told us that a new round of attacks could come soon after Tuesday’s midterms

Trump has also been questioning allies about the job performances of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, two outside advisers close to Trump told us
Hegseth and Caine have been two of Trump’s key counselors on the war
In its earliest stages, they were also among the most publicly optimistic about its prospects—although they haven’t held a press conference since May

Trump often solicits opinions from a kitchen Cabinet of friends outside his administration before making any personnel moves. [ Read: Trump’s gamble to end the Iran war ] Hegseth is not a popular figure in much of the White House

Some close to Trump suggested to us that the defense secretary has not been honest about the state of the war, which he consistently paints in rosy terms to keep Trump happy. “Hegseth is good at telling the president what he wants to hear,” said one of the outside advisers

Sean Parnell, a Pentagon spokesperson, told us in a statement that “Secretary Hegseth always provides the President and White House senior leaders the full operational picture,” calling any suggestion otherwise “dead wrong.” The defense chief has also sought to burnish his standing with the president by pursuing those suspected of leaking to the press, one of the worst transgressions on Trump’s list of personnel offenses
Last week, Hegseth abruptly fired one of the Joint Staff’s most senior officers, Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia, the director of planning
Officials who work for Hegseth said Sylvia failed lie-detector tests related to the disclosure of information to reporters
Sylvia hasn’t commented and couldn’t be reached

Hegseth had ordered Sylvia to undergo at least three polygraphs as part of a broader leak investigation after news reports earlier this year described White House conversations and details about the shortage of munitions caused by the Iran war, the officials told us
Hegseth has decided that the Joint Staff, which reports to Caine, has a problem with leaks, a contention that Caine has not forcefully pushed back on, officials told us
Hegseth’s self-portrayal to Trump allies as having the president’s back resonates with a commander in chief who, since his first term, has suspected senior Pentagon officials of insufficient loyalty

The White House spokesperson Anna Kelly, in a statement to us, gave an endorsement of Hegseth and Caine, praising their work in reshaping the Pentagon and declaring that “President Trump and everyone at the White House have full confidence in both Secretary Hegseth and General Caine, who are fully aligned with the President’s mission.” Caine has appeared largely out of the loop over the alleged misdeeds of one of his own senior staff

When The Atlantic first reported that Sylvia was out, the Joint Staff issued a prewritten statement that thanked Sylvia for his “32 years of distinguished service to our nation.” Caine then learned additional details from the secretary’s team about what exactly had led to Sylvia’s dismissal, while Hegseth returned from a trip from Asia, the officials told us

Hours later, Caine’s office issued a new statement that said the original “did not appropriately reflect the full circumstances.” The Joint Staff said in a statement that the chairman offers “his best military advice and recommendations, along with all associated risks” but “does not publicly discuss these necessarily private conversations with civilian leadership.” That confidentiality protects service members “who are endangered by unacceptable unauthorized disclosures,” the statement added
As the war has dragged on, Trump’s anger has risen over the conflict’s damage to Republicans’ midterm chances
A realization has set in at the White House that Trump is unlikely to pull out another remarkable political comeback in the midterms
The House appears gone, and the Senate may be too

Trump has raged in recent weeks that his messaging is not breaking through, and he now believes that the Iran war is at least in part to blame for his political predicament, the two advisers and an official told us
Not one to take responsibility himself, Trump is searching for a scapegoat, and has focused on those who had told him that a war with Iran would be quick and decisive
Hegseth and Caine were both at the White House last week to present Trump and Vice President Vance with a series of options designed to create the conditions for Trump to declare victory
Admiral Brad Cooper, the top commander at U.S
Central Command, which is responsible for the military’s Middle East operations, was also at the White House last week
Trump now has to decide whether those options, and the advisers who offered them to him, are capable of bringing about a better outcome
T he military options before the president represent a series of unpalatable choices, current and former defense officials familiar with the plans told us
They give the president the chance to order strikes that would last a few hours, a few days, or several weeks
The president could also opt to maintain the U.S. naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz while dangling the threat of a return to action
Advocates for a resumption of strikes believe that the economic pressure campaign is working and that additional military activity would force Tehran to the negotiating table
A lengthy campaign would target Iran’s defenses, as in the war’s early days, before the U.S. shifted its strikes to concentrate on Iranian forces around the Strait of Hormuz
The U.S. is expected to argue that the military is targeting infrastructure that serves both civilian and military purposes
And such attacks could violate international humanitarian law

Another scenario calls for a days-long campaign against Iran’s nuclear program. [ Read: Trump is preparing for a long war ] Many within the administration expect that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose political fate remains uncertain after Israel’s election, would support a resumption of strikes, given his enthusiasm for the war and his belief that it would help him retain power
Even a devastating campaign, though, might not induce concessions from Tehran
The regime could survive the attacks and celebrate its resilience after absorbing another round of U.S. firepower

After the U.S. and Israel staged a weeks-long campaign that began in late February, subsequent short strikes have only hardened Iranian resolve and prompted Tehran to lash out at U.S. assets and allies in the region

And any strike campaign would further deplete munitions stockpiles. “If those strikes don’t work, you’ve now sort of exposed the limits of those strikes,” Michael Cohen, the director of an initiative at the Stimson Center think tank that studies whether U.S. military interventions justify their costs. “You keep hitting them and they don’t back down
So what are you going to keep doing? Keep escalating?” Some in Trump’s orbit hope even the threat of strikes would nudge Iran back to negotiations, though that strategy has failed many times before
Last Sunday, Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s security chief

title: An SNL Sketch to Make Airlines Feel Ashamed
excerpt: For many travelers, flying has become an indignity to endure rather than an experience to enjoy
body: For many travelers, flying has become an indignity to endure rather than an experience to enjoy

Seats are more cramped than ever; flight delays are becoming normalized; somehow, airlines have invented an even worse version of Economy. (Welcome to Basic!) Perhaps most unsettling, though, is the unpredictability of other people on board
Videos of unhinged passengers attempting to open the plane door midair, fighting over reclining seats, shouting slurs, or otherwise disrupting flights have become routine viewing online
This fall, a first-class passenger on an American Airlines flight became violent; he was duct-taped to his seat while the plane made an emergency landing so he could be arrested

Social media tends to make extreme behavior seem more common than it is—although perhaps not in this case: FAA data show that the number of incidents involving unruly fliers has risen sharply since 2019

On last night’s Saturday Night Live , hosted by Inde Navarrette, a layered spoof imagined how a major airline might finally address the stubborn issue of problem passengers in a way that would still benefit its bottom line
In the sketch, a Delta spokesperson, played by Ashley Padilla, acknowledged that these incidents are ticking up
No traveler, she said, should have to deal with a volatile seat neighbor

Padilla then proposed a solution: Delta Disruptive, “a new section of the plane exclusively for crazy people,” available “on all domestic flights within Florida.” This new airline class, she promised brightly, would welcome fliers who refused to sit in their assigned seat, as well as those who insist on smoking, Disney adults who want to chug beers, and passengers yelling their theories about the Illuminati to the entire cabin

Delta Disruptive, Padilla pledged, would provide a space for the “basic, inconsiderate a-hole” as well as the “paranoid lunatic” endangering everyone on board, with a four-inch-thick slab of plexiglass separating it from the rest of the plane
In one testimonial, a passenger played by Mikey Day approvingly noted that the section didn’t make him check his bag, which was clearly never going to fit in the overhead compartment
Scenes depicting growing anarchy showed one passenger rolling a joint and another insistent about licking the toes of a man clipping his toenails in his seat

But don’t worry, Padilla said: To ensure that nothing spun too out of control, the section would be staffed by the “toughest, gayest ex–Spirit Airlines employees who have seen much worse.” One flight attendant, played by Kenan Thompson, threw a man’s “comfort iguana” out of the plane after it wouldn’t stop biting people. [ Read: The only thing worse than Spirit Airlines ] The sketch animated the hellish experience of, say, sitting next to an inappropriate passenger who won’t stop yelling about shadow people
But its deeper and more cynical humor came from slyly hinting at how airlines have evaded recognizing their own complicity in the deterioration of the flying experience
Not that Padilla—whose brittle cheeriness clearly masked an exasperation lurking under the surface—acknowledged any of this

Rather, she saw the ongoing issue of unruly in-flight behavior as yet another opportunity to make a buck. “You see, Delta didn’t want to deal with the constant problems these passengers create, but we still wanted their money,” she confessed
This moment of candor reflects the way that real-life air carriers squeeze money out of every possible scenario on board

On many airlines, even a modicum of comfort now comes at a premium—wanting to travel with a carry-on, for instance, or just drinking a glass of water—a circumstance that may be helping push travelers over the edge, especially as inequality in the air mirrors a sense of economic injustice on the ground

Earlier this year, The Wall Street Journal reported that airlines are reducing the size of economy cabins to make room for expensive lie-flat seats and rows with a few more inches of leg room, giving these companies still more opportunities to charge passengers extra

Additionally, soaring jet-fuel costs, exacerbated by the war with Iran, have caused airfare prices to spike an average of 23 percent since January, according to recent federal data. [ Read: Airlines are just banks now ] Even those who want nothing more than to reach their destination with zero frills may not be safe from price squeezes
A lawsuit filed earlier this year alleged that JetBlue gathered passenger data to set different prices for airfare based on personal information
Passengers who can’t trust their airline are less likely to trust anyone they encounter on their flights—including other passengers
It would take more than a plexiglass partition to solve that problem.

title: Inside the Plan to Send 1,000 DOJ Monitors to the Polls
excerpt: F or more than 60 years , the Department of Justice has sent its attorneys and staff to polling places across the country to ensure that Americans can vote free
body: F or more than 60 years , the Department of Justice has sent its attorneys and staff to polling places across the country to ensure that Americans can vote free of discrimination or intimidation

They’ve watched to see if Black voters were illegally hindered in any way, if those who use a wheelchair or walker could get into facilities, and if those who couldn’t read the ballot for any reason—blindness, lack of English proficiency, or simply not having the skill—had help
Officials selected locations that had had problems in the past or where people had reported concerns

When the feds would show up in the Tucson area of Arizona, where Spanish speakers and retirees are as numerous as the cacti dotting the Sonoran Desert, local officials considered the monitors partners in protecting the right to vote

But ahead of the primary election this past July, when Pima County Elections Director Constance Hargrove learned that DOJ was sending six representatives—most of whom were criminal prosecutors—she became worried

Would they just witness the vote, as in years past, or were they planning to gather evidence to later try to undermine the results? Would they know the basic rules? She told DOJ’s coordinator during a phone call: “Remind them that they cannot take a gun or weapon into the vote centers.” On Primary Day, the monitors’ activities seemed normal, Hargrove told us
But she’s still concerned about the plan to send 1,000 of them to polling locations in every state for Tuesday’s election
The number itself is “a tall order,” Hargrove told us, as most previous administrations—Republican and Democratic—have detailed far fewer
And then there’s this department’s track record on elections
DOJ under President Trump has taken up his years-long quest to prove that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him

Officials have seized ballots in Georgia , gathered material from Arizona, and questioned election officials in Wisconsin—but still have not found evidence of the widespread voter fraud the president has alleged

In recent days, DOJ reminded all state election officials to preserve materials from their elections. “I’m not going to freak myself out before Election Day, or my poll workers, or the voters,” Hargrove said

She has reminded workers to follow their training should the monitors—or anyone else—be disruptive: “You can always call 911.” Her concerns and suspicions are widely shared among the dozen-plus local and state election officials we spoke with across the country

Some worry that a long-standing program created during the civil-rights era to prevent intimidation, particularly of nonwhite voters, could be used as an extension of the administration’s attacks on the democratic process
The officials also said they fear that monitors could misinterpret what they see and then share incomplete or inaccurate information with DOJ that could be used to undermine the results
Pels, a Justice Department spokesperson, strenuously objected to these concerns in a written response to our questions about the program

Pels noted that the election officials we spoke with did not cite an example of “a single voter who was intimidated by a Justice Department monitor.” Should local officials see monitors acting improperly, Pels said, they should report them to DOJ. “The Department has monitored elections for decades, under administrations of both parties

They do not interfere with voting, and they follow state rules on polling place access,” Pels wrote. “Every monitor has the same role: to observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department

The Department will review those concerns after Election Day and act where appropriate.” T his year’s program is overseen by Harmeet Dhillon , the assistant attorney general for the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, who has described monitors as a way “to increase voter confidence, to troubleshoot problems.” Dhillon’s critics have noted her ties to prominent election deniers and her support of legislation limiting mail-in voting
Her division, meanwhile, has sued dozens of state election officials, seeking—so far unsuccessfully—access to voter rolls containing partial Social Security numbers and other sensitive information

The suits are part of a nationwide search for noncitizens who might be illegally voting. “We see a problem, frankly, with some election officials refusing to clean up their voter rolls and knowingly allowing noncitizens, for example, to stay on the voter rolls,” she told Bloomberg . “This is a federal crime.” In a July post on X, Dhillon described the monitor program as aimed at ensuring equal access to the ballot, as it has in the past

But, she said, it will also help make sure that no American’s vote is “cancelled out by someone who shouldn’t be voting.” (Voting by noncitizens is extremely rare, analysis after analysis has found.) Pels, the DOJ spokesperson, told us that its monitors “will not be questioning voters about their citizenship status at the polls.” But Pels added that “if our monitors uncover evidence of such crimes while monitoring, we will use it.” [ Read: The election deniers’ long game ] The Justice Department has recruited criminal prosecutors to participate as monitors

Their inclusion overturns a longtime practice of not using those who have the power to charge people with crimes, and has raised questions about how the Justice Department might use their observations, particularly in places central to criminal investigations into the 2020 election, such as Arizona and Georgia

A former DOJ Civil Rights Division official, who requested anonymity to speak with us out of fear of professional retaliation, told us that previous administrations “never sent prosecutors, because we never wanted to do anything that might scare people.” Pels told us that monitors will not identify themselves as prosecutors
Eric Neff, the acting chief of the Civil Rights Division’s Voting Section, said in a sworn declaration released as part of ongoing litigation that no FBI or ICE employees would serve as monitors

However, employees from the Federal Bureau of Prisons; the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives; and the Drug Enforcement Administration would be involved—a departure from long-held norms, three former DOJ attorneys told us

Pels said that their inclusion is “not new policy” and that they are “not being sent as law enforcement.” To try to understand how the monitors might act on Tuesday, we looked at how they operated during the primaries
Although they watched without incident in many states, that wasn’t the case in deep-red Wyoming

On Primary Day in August, two monitors showed up at a Cheyenne polling place and asked the poll workers “highly unusual” questions that were outside their purview, including about how electronic poll books were acquired and whether they could see the tabulators, according to one local official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of safety concerns
Pels said the monitors’ questions were “routine” and disputed that they’d asked about the procurement of equipment

The local official told us that workers described the monitors as “very assertive,” and that they walked around “like they owned the place.” She added: “If you’re not expecting big, tall, beefy men, it could be rattling.” Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon, a Republican, criticized the monitors’ activities at a public meeting, explaining that just as he doesn’t like the idea of the federal government “taking our guns,” he also dislikes the notion of it “taking our votes.” Pels told us that the Justice Department disagreed “with the public framing” that the monitors were “‘aggressive’ or did anything improper,” and said that Dhillon “had a cordial meeting” after the primary with the governor, the state attorney general, and a county election clerk. [ Read: The supporters urging Trump to declare martial law for the midterms ] We submitted roughly 200 public-records requests to states, counties, cities, and towns over the past several weeks, seeking to learn more about DOJ’s plan and the people carrying it out
Those records, along with our conversations with election officials, reflected that nearly all of the monitors’ visits during the primaries were professional
Some monitors asked poll workers about their training; some talked with voters outside polling locations
DOJ coordinated with local officials, advising when the monitors would arrive and what they could expect from them

A DOJ lawyer recently wrote to the lieutenant governor of Utah with an assurance that the program would run “the same way as in the past,” according to correspondence that we obtained. “Monitors follow all rules of the state and jurisdiction
Monitors dress in business casual clothing

No uniforms or pins identifying as DOJ are allowed.” But a meeting a few days ago between DOJ and Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes, a Democrat, reflected fears that this year’s election won’t be business as usual

During the conversation, which state officials told DOJ they were recording, Fontes asked why he should believe that the monitors are working in a nonpartisan manner, given the department’s recent lawsuit seeking to decertify Alaska’s Senate results if the Democratic candidate wins, according to audio of the meeting we reviewed. “It’s pretty patently obvious that a lawsuit filed based on a political outcome puts the department in a compromised position,” Fontes told the DOJ attorneys, who said they are sending roughly 20 monitors to the Phoenix area, plus more around the state
The DOJ officials replied that the monitors are, and would, remain nonpartisan
Fontes also asked if the monitors could be called to testify about their observations in court—as witnesses

title: The MAGA Reckoning Arrives
excerpt: I n the first months of Donald Trump’s first term, as one moral outrage followed another, I often found myself repeating, in conversation, a seven-word phrase:
body: I n the first months of Donald Trump’s first term, as one moral outrage followed another, I often found myself repeating, in conversation, a seven-word phrase: Where there’s no bottom, there’s no bottom
However bad things got, they were bound to get worse
That applied above all to Trump, but also to his party, which was fusing with him
We’ve since seen endless examples of what “no bottom” looks like
The latest is an ad from Vivek Ramaswamy, who is running for governor of Ohio
It features the estranged mother of Ramaswamy’s opponent, Amy Acton, calling her daughter a liar about her childhood and urging Ohioans not to vote for her
Here is what we know about that childhood
In 1978, when Acton was 12, her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was indicted for raping her
He fled to Pennsylvania, where he died as a fugitive in 2004
Acton and her brother were removed from their mother’s custody, and she has not spoken with her mother since
Her mother, Donna Arthur, stayed married to the man charged with raping her daughter until he died
The Ramaswamy campaign pledged to spend $4 million to air the ad on television and online

Some Republicans objected; Ohio’s current governor, Mike DeWine, called the ad “ deeply, deeply troubling .” But the two most important Republicans in the country, Trump and Vice President Vance, defended it

Trump called it “very powerful” and wrote , “Who wouldn’t use such an Ad? I would, it’s called, ‘hitting pay dirt.’” Vance said he was “a little bit disgusted”—not by the ad but by the Republicans “whining” about it
This is what family values look like to Republicans in the Trump era
A s a young conservative in the 1980s, among my formative influences were Gertrude Himmelfarb and Irving Kristol, Allan Bloom and Leon Kass, James Q
Bennett, Peter Berger and Richard John Neuhaus, and Michael Novak

I was especially shaped by George Will’s 1983 book, Statecraft as Soulcraft: What Government Does , which argued that statecraft is inherently “soulcraft,” the cultivation of public spirit and moral sensibilities

These thinkers shared the conviction that self-government depends on what Kristol called “republican virtue.” They believed, too, that norms are fragile and that the membrane separating civilization from barbarism is thin
Character and conscience need to be cultivated
Public discourse either elevates or degrades, moving us away from or closer to a will-to-power ethic
The conduct of leaders, including political leaders, is educative
And when deviancy becomes widespread, we grow used to it

It was a Democrat, Daniel Patrick Moynihan, who coined the phrase defining deviancy down , by which he meant that a society overwhelmed by destructive behavior lowers its standards rather than confronting it
None of this means that conservatives, or the Republican Party, were paragons of virtue
These thinkers and those who were influenced by their work often fell short of what they preached
But their aspirations were ennobling, and some of them lived lives that matched their words
Today the American right is not merely indifferent to character formation; it is in the business of character deformation
The Ramaswamy ad embodies the “no bottom” ethic of the Trump-era GOP, and its wickedness comes in layers
C ruelty and coarseness have momentum, but they also have limits
Political leaders who relentlessly push brutality do lower a nation’s standards, at least for a time
But if we’re fortunate, they also awaken its conscience
The revulsion comes first, almost physical, like bile rising in the throat
It is what Kass, in a different context, called “ the wisdom of repugnance .” The reckoning follows
The anti-MAGA reckoning may have finally begun, though much later than it should have
His hold on his own base is weakening; its members, like everyone else, are suffering because of the staggering incompetence of the president
And many of those who continue to support Trump are exhausted
In Ohio, a GOP poll shows that the Ramaswamy ad is backfiring
Axios reports that by a 2-to-1 ratio, those who said they were familiar with it said it made them more likely to vote for Acton
A true repudiation of the politics of savagery will require a rebuke from voters in every region of America

title: I Thought I’d Left Authoritarianism Behind
excerpt: L ate in the summer of 1984 , I met my dying father for what I thought would be our last lunch together
body: L ate in the summer of 1984 , I met my dying father for what I thought would be our last lunch together
We’d chosen one of his favorite restaurants in downtown Brno, the capital of Moravia in what was then Communist Czechoslovakia
The ceiling fans spun sluggishly in the air; the clatter of plates echoed off the marble walls and high ceilings; cigarette smoke curled above tables where men spoke in whispers
My father looked thinner than I’d remembered him
Cancer had hollowed his cheeks and deepened the furrows at his eyes
But it wasn’t only illness that appeared to weigh on him
He seemed lost in his thoughts—haunted, perhaps, by more than his failing body
I had invited him because I carried a secret
As the waiter set down our favorite dish—broiled trout with herb butter and country potatoes—I looked around to make sure that no one was sitting close enough to overhear us
Then, my hands trembling slightly, I leaned in and told him that I was planning to defect
A close friend of mine from architecture school had been found dead under suspicious circumstances

Many of those close to him believed that thugs from the StB—the regime’s secret police—had murdered him after he’d refused to spy on a relative in Rome who’d been labeled an “enemy of the state.” It was clear that to protect the authoritarian regime, the government would kill even innocent people who refused to collaborate
I could not breathe inside that system any longer
I was ready to risk everything to escape. [ Read: Authoritarians are great at propaganda—until they’re not ] I braced for my father’s reaction
I expected anger, or for him to enumerate a litany of horrors that might await me if I were caught
I could end up in jail for years, and then would be blacklisted by the regime from jobs, housing, educational opportunities, and more
Our entire family, including my father, despite a spotless political career, could also be punished
He studied me for what felt like an eternity

When he finally spoke, his voice was calm, almost tender. “I understand,” he said. “And I support you.” After another long silence, he leaned forward, lowering his voice so that the waiter could not hear
For decades, he said, he had lived a double life—outwardly a loyal Communist, but in actuality a spy for the West
The man I knew as a gentle gardener, an enthusiastic party member, and a dutiful bureaucrat had been risking his life to undermine the regime that he’d pretended to serve
He spoke of clandestine meetings in parks and hotel bars in faraway countries, of documents copied and smuggled, of narrow escapes when he suspected that his cover was blown
He had never told anyone before me—not even my mother
She had despised the Communists and had eventually divorced him because she believed that he had become one of them
He knew that to reveal the truth would have endangered her, my sister, and me
For my father, unburdening himself of his secret was an act of release; for me, the moment was a revelation
Until then, I had regarded my father as an inscrutable man shaped by the compromises of totalitarian life
Now I was finally seeing the moral steel beneath the surface
His calm was not complacency; it was discipline
My father was an idealist who had risked everything for the hope of restoring freedom that had been lost—and that I, too, was seeking
Sitting motionless in that dining room, the restaurant seeming to fade around me, I realized that my father’s confession was also a farewell
He knew that, once I fled, we might never meet again
Soon I would begin my journey to a new homeland, one where, I was convinced, I would be able to leave the authoritarianism of my past behind me
M y father had been born in free Czechoslovakia between the two world wars, into a country that was proud of its democracy and culture
But in February 1948, everything had changed
The Communist Party, riding the wave of Soviet triumph over the Nazi occupation, engineered a coup

The new regime followed the dictator’s playbook to the letter, replacing competent officials with loyal sycophants; censoring the independent media and flooding the public with propaganda; seizing control of the courts, military, and police; and quickly dividing the nation into “us” and “them.” By the time I was born, about a decade later, totalitarianism had saturated the very air we breathed

At school, we memorized slogans about the wisdom of the party and the danger of “imperialist enemies within and abroad.” Neighbors whispered carefully in stairwells, or spoke in code; even family members sometimes informed on one another
The price of a careless remark could be a job, a degree, or one’s freedom
Most people survived by performing obedience

title: Parents, let your kids eat as much candy as they want – less restriction could help reduce the urge to overeat
url:
<title>Parents, let your kids eat as much candy as they want – less restriction could help reduce the urge to overeat</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769155/original/file-20261029-64-91eisb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Candy becomes less special when it&#39;s not a &#39;bad&#39; food you can&#39;t have.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/portrait-of-girl-crossing-eyes-with-lollipop-in-royalty-free-image/585283527">Peter Muller/Connect Images via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Kids and candy are a classic pairing. From trick-or-treating to Easter baskets, to local parades and birthday parties, it can feel like kids are almost always bringing home another bag of treats. But while these holidays and events may be exciting for kids, they often end with parents dreading what comes next: negotiations around how much candy to consume. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://miamioh.edu/profiles/ehs/bryn-beeder.html">registered dietitian</a> and mom of three, I understand the stress that comes with wanting to encourage healthy food choices without removing all the fun of childhood traditions. I also believe the answer to this dilemma may be simpler than the familiar back and forth of “Just one more piece of candy!” and “Haven’t you had enough already?”</p>

<p>Research suggests that by managing the candy inventory less and encouraging more autonomy around sweets, parents can help their kids practice <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appet.2020.105060">tapping into their hunger and fullness cues</a>, promoting a healthier relationship with food over time. </p>

<h2>Making food moral</h2>

<p>There is no question that some foods have greater nutritional value than others. A piece of cake – carrot cake included – will never provide the vitamins and minerals of a large garden salad. As a result, people often categorize different foods as “good” or “bad.” </p>

<p>The tendency to place food in two polarizing buckets can affect everything from what foods you purchase at the grocery store to the language you use to describe food. The problem is, “<a href="https://www.allianceforeatingdisorders.com/removing-food-morality/">good” and “bad” are moral concepts</a>. When morality is consistently applied to food, a person’s relationship to food can become complicated. Instead of viewing food as fueling, it can become a measuring stick for whether your food choices are something to feel proud of or guilty about.</p>

<p>When a person’s inner monologue about food is preoccupied with whether it is good or bad for their health or diet plan, food choices can become less about enjoyment and more about their <a href="https://www.urmc.rochester.edu/news/publications/health-matters/why-we-need-to-get-past-food-morality">willpower to make the “right” decision</a> at the grocery store and at mealtimes. Any guilt or shame that comes from this evaluation can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eatbeh.2024.101848">spill over into what foods are served</a> freely at home and which are restricted.</p>

<h2>Restriction leads to overeating</h2>

<p>The idea of food restriction often sounds punishing. For parents and others who take care of children, food restriction often may simply be an attempt to limit sugary foods and introduce more fruits and vegetables.</p>

<p>But for kids, restricting certain foods may lead them to become <a href="https://www.health.harvard.edu/diet-and-nutrition/understanding-food-noise-and-how-to-turn-down-the-volume">preoccupied with those foods</a>. They may be nagged by the knowledge that the foods adults often call “bad” are also the ones that are really delicious. What started as a simple candy rule can continue to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/ajcn/78.2.215">influence a child’s relationship to food and eating</a> long after the treats are gone. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769158/original/file-20261029-64-qwx40m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Person holding a gummy bear and signing 'one' at a child with their hands on the top of their hand in protest or disappointment" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769158/original/file-20261029-64-qwx40m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769158/original/file-20261029-64-qwx40m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769158/original/file-20261029-64-qwx40m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769158/original/file-20261029-64-qwx40m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769158/original/file-20261029-64-qwx40m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769158/original/file-20261029-64-qwx40m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769158/original/file-20261029-64-qwx40m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Restricting certain foods can lead to increased preoccupation with those very foods.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/teaching-moderation-and-sugar-control-in-childhood-royalty-free-image/2270431595">Oscar Requejo/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Parents often approach food restriction in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appet.2025.108330">two different ways</a>. In overt food restriction, kids are aware that their parents or guardians are limiting access to specific foods because they can see it or are told specific foods are off limits. In practice, this might mean the kids know candy is in the house but stored out of reach in the kitchen cupboards. Parents or caregivers who practice covert food restriction, on the other hand, may choose to not buy bags of candy at all in order to encourage more balanced food choices.</p>

<p>Research suggests that overt restriction can unintentionally increase kids’ <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appet.2025.108330">interest in those restricted food items</a>. That preoccupation may mean the child has a more difficult time listening to their fullness cues when presented with those foods. If bags of candy are usually stored out of reach, it may be tempting to eat more than just a few pieces when access is finally granted – and they may completely ignore any signs that their body is full.</p>

<h2>Intuitive eating for kids</h2>

<p>Incorporating neutral language about food at mealtimes and encouraging kids to eat according to their own hunger and fullness cues can help them <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/15598276241279223">build trust in their bodies and improve family connection</a> at the table. Taking the pressure off finishing all the food on the plate can instead place emphasis on savoring the sensory experience of each bite.</p>

<p>Eating according to internal cues is one part of <a href="https://www.intuitiveeating.org/about-us/10-principles-of-intuitive-eating/">intuitive eating</a>, which aims to increase a person’s trust in their own body to signal when to start eating and when to stop. Kids can also benefit from this same framework, with some age-appropriate modifications.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.ellynsatterinstitute.org/how-to-feed/division-of-responsibility/">Satter Division of Responsibility in Feeding</a> provides a simple, research-based approach to feeding kids in a way that avoids power struggles between kids and caretakers at the table. Developed by the Ellyn Satter Institute, a nonprofit focused on improving people’s relationship to food, the goal of the framework is to introduce intuitive eating in a kid-friendly way. When providing food through this approach, parents decide when and what food is served, while kids are in charge of deciding what and how much they eat from their plates. The emphasis is on helping kids eat according to their internal cues without pressuring them to eat specific foods.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769162/original/file-20261029-64-hdflt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Three children sit around table of food outside" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769162/original/file-20261029-64-hdflt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769162/original/file-20261029-64-hdflt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769162/original/file-20261029-64-hdflt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769162/original/file-20261029-64-hdflt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769162/original/file-20261029-64-hdflt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=565&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769162/original/file-20261029-64-hdflt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=565&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769162/original/file-20261029-64-hdflt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=565&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Giving kids more autonomy in what they eat during meals is a way of practicing intuitive eating.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/children-having-lunch-in-the-outside-royalty-free-image/168917690">Michael H/DigitalVision via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Candy can be a part of the menu rotation in this feeding framework. Repeatedly exposing kids to a variety of foods, including sugary treats outside of special holidays or events, means no food becomes emphasized for being better or worse than another food – it is <a href="https://theconversation.com/all-foods-can-fit-in-a-balanced-diet-a-dietitian-explains-how-flexibility-can-be-healthier-than-dieting-270049">all simply food</a>. </p>

<p>This approach can shift the conversation to how different foods affect their bodies in different ways: Some food – like candy – makes them run super fast, some foods grow their muscles, while other foods keep their eyes strong.  </p>

<h2>Building healthier relationships with food</h2>

<p>Regularly using neutral language to describe food and exposing kids to a variety of foods helps reduce the power that sugary treats have over their appetites. This doesn’t mean birthday cake, doughnuts and candy will no longer taste delicious. It simply means children can rest assured they will see their favorite treats again without the added urge to overconsume them.  </p>

<p>If you’re interested in exploring how intuitive eating principles could change your child’s or your own relationship with food, here are a few practices you can try at home:</p>

<p><strong>Involve children in <a href="https://health.clevelandclinic.org/how-to-overcome-your-childs-picky-eating-habits">menu planning and grocery shopping</a></strong>. Let your kids pick a treat to add to a few meals each week, and serve the treat with the rest of the food on the menu for that day. <a href="https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/how-can-you-help-your-child-practice-intuitive-eating/">Presenting all food items at the same time</a> on the plate – versus saving a dessert or treat for after the meal – visually reminds everyone that food does not have to be earned. Rather, each food nourishes their bodies in different ways. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769151/original/file-20261029-64-k6kyze.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Smiling child dragging smiling adult by the hand to bulk food shelves in grocery store" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769151/original/file-20261029-64-k6kyze.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769151/original/file-20261029-64-k6kyze.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769151/original/file-20261029-64-k6kyze.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769151/original/file-20261029-64-k6kyze.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769151/original/file-20261029-64-k6kyze.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769151/original/file-20261029-64-k6kyze.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769151/original/file-20261029-64-k6kyze.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Try giving kids a say on what you pick up during grocery trips.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/family-outing-to-the-grocery-store-royalty-free-image/920889348">FatCamera/E+ via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><strong>Avoid commenting on what your kids eat</strong>. It can be tempting to praise a child when they choose to take a bite of the broccoli you’ve been encouraging for weeks.  Praising kids for eating certain foods versus others can create a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appet.2026.108719">food hierarchy</a>, leading them to think about food as a way to earn a reward instead of fueling their body.</p>

<p><strong>Challenge your own relationship with food</strong>. Do you eat when you are hungry and stop when you are full? Do you restrict your own food cravings as a punishment, or do you struggle to control yourself when eating a treat you love? Kids are always watching, and your own food behaviors often speak louder than words.</p>

<p><strong>Consider letting your kids indulge for a day</strong>. In my own family, I don’t limit how much candy my three kids eat on Halloween night. I won’t lie – they usually eat quite a bit. When they mention a stomachache afterward, we talk about how eating a lot of candy can make their bodies feel – without adding judgment. Their interest typically fades over the next few days while we continue to offer a piece of two with meals. Eventually the extras become props for elaborate trick-or-treat pretend play.</p>

<p>One day or evening of holiday eating <a href="https://theconversation.com/dont-stress-out-about-overeating-during-the-holidays-a-dietitian-explains-how-a-day-of-indulgence-wont-harm-your-overall-health-269240">does not define their health</a>, but fun memories with friends and families can last a lifetime. So let them eat … candy!</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294113/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <summary>Restricting access to candy is one way parents try to teach their kids moderation. But this can backfire and harm a child’s relationship to food and eating in the long run.</summary>
    <author>
      <name>Bryn Beeder, Assistant Clinical Lecturer in Kinesiology, Nutrition, and Health, Miami University</name>
