excerpt: Candy becomes less special when it's not a 'bad' food you can't have
body: Candy becomes less special when it's not a 'bad' food you can't have
Peter Muller/Connect Images via Getty Images Kids and candy are a classic pairing
From trick-or-treating to Easter baskets, to local parades and birthday parties, it can feel like kids are almost always bringing home another bag of treats
But while these holidays and events may be exciting for kids, they often end with parents dreading what comes next: negotiations around how much candy to consume
As a registered dietitian and mom of three, I understand the stress that comes with wanting to encourage healthy food choices without removing all the fun of childhood traditions

I also believe the answer to this dilemma may be simpler than the familiar back and forth of “Just one more piece of candy!” and “Haven’t you had enough already?” Research suggests that by managing the candy inventory less and encouraging more autonomy around sweets, parents can help their kids practice tapping into their hunger and fullness cues , promoting a healthier relationship with food over time
Making food moral There is no question that some foods have greater nutritional value than others
A piece of cake – carrot cake included – will never provide the vitamins and minerals of a large garden salad

As a result, people often categorize different foods as “good” or “bad.” The tendency to place food in two polarizing buckets can affect everything from what foods you purchase at the grocery store to the language you use to describe food
The problem is, “ good” and “bad” are moral concepts
When morality is consistently applied to food, a person’s relationship to food can become complicated
Instead of viewing food as fueling, it can become a measuring stick for whether your food choices are something to feel proud of or guilty about

When a person’s inner monologue about food is preoccupied with whether it is good or bad for their health or diet plan, food choices can become less about enjoyment and more about their willpower to make the “right” decision at the grocery store and at mealtimes
Any guilt or shame that comes from this evaluation can spill over into what foods are served freely at home and which are restricted
Restriction leads to overeating The idea of food restriction often sounds punishing
For parents and others who take care of children, food restriction often may simply be an attempt to limit sugary foods and introduce more fruits and vegetables
But for kids, restricting certain foods may lead them to become preoccupied with those foods
They may be nagged by the knowledge that the foods adults often call “bad” are also the ones that are really delicious
What started as a simple candy rule can continue to influence a child’s relationship to food and eating long after the treats are gone
Restricting certain foods can lead to increased preoccupation with those very foods
Oscar Requejo/iStock via Getty Images Plus Parents often approach food restriction in two different ways
In overt food restriction, kids are aware that their parents or guardians are limiting access to specific foods because they can see it or are told specific foods are off limits
In practice, this might mean the kids know candy is in the house but stored out of reach in the kitchen cupboards
Parents or caregivers who practice covert food restriction, on the other hand, may choose to not buy bags of candy at all in order to encourage more balanced food choices
Research suggests that overt restriction can unintentionally increase kids’ interest in those restricted food items
That preoccupation may mean the child has a more difficult time listening to their fullness cues when presented with those foods

If bags of candy are usually stored out of reach, it may be tempting to eat more than just a few pieces when access is finally granted – and they may completely ignore any signs that their body is full

Intuitive eating for kids Incorporating neutral language about food at mealtimes and encouraging kids to eat according to their own hunger and fullness cues can help them build trust in their bodies and improve family connection at the table
Taking the pressure off finishing all the food on the plate can instead place emphasis on savoring the sensory experience of each bite
Eating according to internal cues is one part of intuitive eating , which aims to increase a person’s trust in their own body to signal when to start eating and when to stop
Kids can also benefit from this same framework, with some age-appropriate modifications
The Satter Division of Responsibility in Feeding provides a simple, research-based approach to feeding kids in a way that avoids power struggles between kids and caretakers at the table
Developed by the Ellyn Satter Institute, a nonprofit focused on improving people’s relationship to food, the goal of the framework is to introduce intuitive eating in a kid-friendly way
When providing food through this approach, parents decide when and what food is served, while kids are in charge of deciding what and how much they eat from their plates
The emphasis is on helping kids eat according to their internal cues without pressuring them to eat specific foods
Giving kids more autonomy in what they eat during meals is a way of practicing intuitive eating
Michael H/DigitalVision via Getty Images Candy can be a part of the menu rotation in this feeding framework

Repeatedly exposing kids to a variety of foods, including sugary treats outside of special holidays or events, means no food becomes emphasized for being better or worse than another food – it is all simply food

This approach can shift the conversation to how different foods affect their bodies in different ways: Some food – like candy – makes them run super fast, some foods grow their muscles, while other foods keep their eyes strong

Building healthier relationships with food Regularly using neutral language to describe food and exposing kids to a variety of foods helps reduce the power that sugary treats have over their appetites

title: Can’t commit to vegetarianism but want animals to suffer less? You’ve got options.
excerpt: Editor’s note, November 1, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary
body: Editor’s note, November 1, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary
The one below was originally published in August 2025
This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas
It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other
I typically eat vegetarian, and have considered going fully vegan out of concern for animal welfare

But lately my on-again, off-again gastrointestinal problems have been acting up, and I’ve had to go back on a more restricted diet to manage my symptoms — no spice, no garlic or onions, nothing acidic, and nothing caffeinated
Sticking to a “bland” diet is hard enough, but doing so while vegetarian is very difficult when things like tomatoes and onions and grapefruits are off the table
I know a lot of people with these issues eat fish or meat, and some medical professionals recommend drinking chicken bone broth to soothe flare-ups
I don’t want to abandon my commitment to animal welfare while my gut sorts itself out, but my food options are limited right now
How should I approach this? Dear Would-Be Vegetarian,  You’re not alone in finding it hard to stick to a purely vegetarian diet
Only 5 percent of American adults say they’re vegetarian or vegan
What’s more, one study found that 84 percent of people who adopt those diets actually go back to eating meat at some point
And most of them aren’t even dealing with the gastrointestinal problems you face.  So, it speaks to the depth of your moral commitment that you’re really wrestling with this

I’ll have some concrete suggestions for you in a bit, but first I want to emphasize that how you approach the question of meat-eating will depend on your underlying moral theory.  There’s a classic split in moral philosophy between deontologists and utilitarians

A deontologist is someone who thinks an action is moral if it’s fulfilling a duty — and we have universal duties like, “always treat others as ends in themselves, never as means to an end.” From that perspective, killing an animal for food would be inherently morally wrong, because you’re treating the animal as a means to an end.  Meanwhile, a utilitarian is someone who thinks that an action is moral if it produces good consequences — and behaving morally means producing the most happiness or well-being possible, or reducing the most suffering possible

Utilitarian philosophers like Peter Singer argue that we should be reducing, and ideally eliminating, the suffering that animals endure at our hands.  Deontologists and utilitarians are often pitted against each other, but they actually have one big thing in common: They both believe in a universal moral principle — whether it’s “always treat others as ends in themselves” or “always maximize happiness.”  A lot of people find that comforting, because it offers certainty about how we should act

Even if acting morally requires hard sacrifices, it’s incredibly soothing to think, “If I just do X, then I’ll know for sure that I’m being a good person!” But these moral theories assume that all the complexity of human life can be reduced to one tidy formula

Can it, really?  Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column? Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions
Sign up here! Another school of philosophy — pragmatism — says we should be skeptical of fixed moral principles

Human life is so complicated, with many different factors at play in any ethical dilemma, so we should be pluralistic about what makes outcomes valuable instead of acting like the only thing that matters is maximizing a single value (say, happiness)
And human society is always evolving, so a moral idea that makes sense in one context may no longer make sense in a different context
To a pragmatist, moral truths are contingent, not universal and unchanging.  I think one pragmatist who can really help you out is the University of Michigan’s Elizabeth Anderson

In a 2005 essay applying pragmatism to the question of eating meat , the philosopher points out that for most of human history, we couldn’t have survived and thrived without killing or exploiting animals for food, transportation, and energy

The social conditions for granting animals moral rights didn’t really exist on a mass scale until recently (although certain non-Western societies did ascribe moral worth to some animals). “The possibility of moralizing our relations to animals (other than our pets),” Anderson writes, “has come to us only lately, and even then not to us all, and not with respect to all animal species.” In other words, Anderson doesn’t think there’s some universal rule like “eating animals is inherently morally wrong.” It’s our social and technological circumstances that have made us more able than before to see animals as part of our moral circle
She also doesn’t believe there’s a single yardstick —  like sentience or intelligence — by which we can judge how much of our moral concern an animal deserves
That’s because moral evaluation isn’t just about animals’ intrinsic capacities, but also about their relationships to us
It matters whether we’ve made them dependent on us by domesticating them, say, or whether they live independently in the wild .  It also matters whether they’re fundamentally hostile to us
Killing bedbugs? Totally fine! They may be sentient, but, Anderson writes, “We are in a permanent state of war with them, without possibility of negotiating for peace
To one-sidedly accommodate their interests…would amount to surrender.” Anderson’s point is not that animals’ intelligence and sentience don’t matter
It’s that lots of other things matter, too, including our own ability to thrive
With this pragmatic approach in mind, you can consider how to balance your concern for animal welfare with your concern for your own welfare

Instead of thinking in terms of a moral absolute that would force you into a “purist” diet no matter the cost to you, you can consider a “reducetarian” diet, which allows you to ease your own struggle while also taking care for animals seriously.  The key thing to realize is that some types of animal consumption cause a lot less suffering than others.  For one thing, if you’re eating meat, try to buy the pasture-raised kind and not the kind that comes from factory farms — the huge industrialized facilities that supply 99 percent of America’s meat
In these facilities, animals are tightly packed together and live under unbelievably harsh and unsanitary conditions
They’re also often mutilated without pain relief : think pigs being castrated, cows being dehorned, and hens being debeaked
Oh, and chickens have been bred to be so big that they’re in constant pain ; they live miserable lives from start to finish

A pasture-raised label doesn’t mean an animal has been spared all of the harms of modern agriculture — it doesn’t guarantee that pain relief is used for painful procedures, and farm animals across different production systems have been bred to maximize production, which can take a toll on their welfare
And of course they’ll ultimately meet the same fate as those raised on factory farms — slaughter
But your goal here is to meaningfully reduce, not 100 percent eliminate, the harms
And at least pasture-raised animals have gotten to roam around in a field and engage in natural behaviors up until the end
It’s a similar story for fish, by the way

title: Are you over-optimizing your hobbies?
excerpt: National Trust gardener Emily Taylor-Ryan arranges an autumn pumpkin and squash display in the village of Taplow in Buckinghamshire, England, on October 22, 202
body: National Trust gardener Emily Taylor-Ryan arranges an autumn pumpkin and squash display in the village of Taplow in Buckinghamshire, England, on October 22, 2026. | Jonathan Brady/PA Images via Getty Images We often pick up hobbies to add some fun to our lives
We join a book group, take up knitting, or commit to finally learning how to play pickleball

But before long, what started out as leisure can begin to feel like just another obligation to execute and perfect: We fall behind in the reading, can’t stop dropping stitches, or the tournament schedule gets overwhelming
It’s a tale as old as time, or at least as old as the United States

Our obsession with productivity may feel new, especially when it crosses over to our hobbies, but according to Gary Cross, a historian and author of the book Free Time: The History of an Elusive Ideal , Americans have been trying to make the most of our time for a while now. “A lot of it is that old Protestant work ethic that was part of the early migration to the United States,” he told Vox. “They were predominantly Protestant Christians who saw work as a kind of a special calling from God.” As Cross explains, this attitude kicked into high gear alongside industrialization. “The capitalists really were all about increasing productivity
Time away from work begins to be seen as in some ways wasted time,” Cross said
And when the labor movement helped win workers some free time for hobbies around the turn of the 20th century, the same mentality made the jump into our leisure time

That time is something that writer Jenny Odell has thought a lot about and explored in her books Saving Time: Discovering a Life Beyond the Clock and H ow to Do Nothing: Resisting the Attention Economy .  “I think both of my books came out of observing the daily experience that I and the people I knew were having, where our relationship to time felt so painful — this unending intensity that was so exhausting,” she said. “There has to be another way.” Odell says that one of the ways to shift our relationship with time is through cultivating hobbies — without falling into the trap of relentless quantification and optimization

So how do we learn to truly enjoy our leisure time, and why should we all consider failing a little more along the way? We learn that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.  Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Odell, edited for length and clarity
You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts
If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545
How is our pursuit of hobbies connected to how we think about time? Hobbies are a place where you can see different ways of thinking about time battling each other
There’s a very fine line between someone who pursues a hobby for the sake of doing it versus someone who feels that they need to optimize it, perhaps even make money off of it
There’s nothing wrong with that, but these are different ways of thinking about the activity that you’re doing
People read the title How to Do Nothing and they think that I’m a person who literally doesn’t do anything
I love to do things and I love to learn things
I think a lot of people start hobbies because they want to learn.  In American culture, a lot of us stop being given opportunities to learn after we’re children or after we’re students
I think it’s really beautiful that adults seek out ways to learn, often leaning into communities where they’re learning with other people

You do get better at things when you learn them.  My feeling is just that that sense of forward movement and learning gets co-opted by this larger culture that we exist in that is also very American: needing to have something to show for your time
What starts out as wanting to learn something turns into something that you’re giving yourself a score on, without your ever having decided to do that
I spoke with a historian who said part of the reason that we relate to our free time in this particular way in America specifically is the history of the Protestant work ethic
How do you help yourself break out of that mentality? I have to shout out this book called The Score by C
In that book he talks about games and how when you play a game, you take on a whole new set of values, and you do that for whatever couple of hours and then you put it away

It’s kind of this practice in taking values, putting them on, taking them off, putting them away.  For me, either literally playing games or trying to have a more playful, experimental mindset about what it is that I’m doing can break that cycle
When you get closer to [a goal], it gets more and more seductive
Like “I want a higher number.” You just need something to break you out of that and be like, “What is this number even measuring?”  For me, I’m a writer
You think you want more words per day, but all words are not the same
There have been moments where I was trying to optimize words per day
I have to stop myself and think about what other ways I could value the situation
Like, “What were those words? Did I make some sort of breakthrough?”  There’s all these other different ways that you could think about what it is that you’re doing
Something I think a lot about when it comes to hobbies is failure
For instance, I’m getting back into photography
I did film photography in high school and this year I picked it back up with the goal to shoot a roll of film per month.  The year’s almost over
I’ve done three rolls of film, one of which I must have unloaded incorrectly because it was completely blown out
What role does failure play in our hobbies and how we interact with that? I love failure
I think it’s so underrated and games are very useful here
A good sports person is open to failure and knows that that’s fun
I think that along with not having opportunities to learn as adults, we also aren’t given opportunities to fail
That’s probably been the case for a long time, but now with social media and things being more visible for a lot of people, we really are not used to failing
I feel like I am actively now seeking out things that I’m bad at just so I can have that feeling

title: Will Melania Trump save Ukraine?
excerpt: Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump arrive for the 80th session of the UN General Assembly in New York City on September 23, 2025. | Alexi J
body: Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump arrive for the 80th session of the UN General Assembly in New York City on September 23, 2025. | Alexi J

Rosenfeld/Getty Images In the last month or so, President Donald Trump’s on-again-off-again relationship with Ukraine — which has ranged from kicking Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy out of the White House in early 2025 to promising new air defense missiles this summer — has once again run cold
Trump has excoriated Zelenskyy for successful Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil and gas infrastructure , called for Zelenskyy’s ouster, and gifted Russia a sanctions reprieve
Trump also hasn’t had much success brokering a ceasefire, much less an end to the war (an announced “energy ceasefire” fell apart-near instantly earlier in October)
She reportedly played a (limited) role in arranging a partial ceasefire for the frontline Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which has been hit especially hard by the war and is currently occupied by Russia
The pause, which is scheduled to run through the weekend, allows food and aid to get in and for a civilian evacuation

While limited, it also shows that both Ukraine and Russia are potentially willing to come to the negotiating table.  After the Trump-Vladimir Putin rapprochement, though, some critics worry that the US is more likely to take Russia’s side — or at least step away from Ukraine’s — both in the war and in any possible peace talks.  To break down what the Trumps are up to, how serious the concerns of Trump abandoning Ukraine for Putin actually are, and what could come next, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Alex Ward , a national security reporter for the Wall Street Journal
Below is an excerpt of Sean’s conversation with Ward, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Let’s start with the most unexpected news out of this war in recent days: that Melania Trump brokered a ceasefire
I’m going to personally, without too much reporting, say that it was probably more Pope Leo
Melania stole Pope Leo’s ceasefire? I think a little bit
Look, this ceasefire is not a small thing
It is a humanitarian ceasefire in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky

The critics would say this allows the Russians to re-arm and regroup, and I guess at the same time also the Ukrainians.  The question is, does it actually have that much influence over the war? No, it’s a very, very small targeted ceasefire
But it is a potential signal that deals can be made.  The Russians are very much saying, look at Melania Trump, look at how important she was to all this

And if I’m the Russians, I would love to be saying things like that because then President Trump feels like the Russians are being very generous towards my wife and to my family, and therefore I side with them.  It feels very convenient that the Russians are pumping that up and that even the White House is pumping up Melania Trump’s influence

When did she become a negotiator in this war? From the beginning, she has been trying to get children kidnapped by Russia back to Ukraine.  That has been a major focus of hers in this war.  Is she the driving force behind this ceasefire? Is she the number one reason it happened? It’s totally possible
There’s just a lot of skepticism out there about whether Kyiv and Moscow were brought to the table and browbeaten by the First Lady
Again, very possible, but both sides, being Ukraine and Russia, have an incentive to play up her role
The ceasefire is just relegated to one city
How come? That’s all they could agree to

If we’re looking at this war at a bigger scale, there’s been a massive discussion about how to get an end to the Ukraine-Russia war.  The US last week was able to broker a commitment to have trilateral talks between the Ukrainians, Russians, and the Americans with the goal toward ending the war
And you’ve heard President Zelenskyy of Ukraine say, “We can call it ceasefire
We can call freeze the conflict.”  Putin goes, ‘No, thank you

I would like basically a handover of the territory that I want, even though I’ve been unable to conquer it after nearly five years.’ It’s unclear if they’re even going to get into the room for those trilateral negotiations

Even if they do, it’ll probably be at a lower technical level.  So are we ever going to get to the point that Putin and Zelenskyy and Trump get in a room, all hold hands and say ‘war over’? I highly doubt it, but that is the goal they’re after

You see the Trump administration, the Kremlin, and Kyiv all point to this Oleshky ceasefire as, like, ‘Hey, this could be a model for the much bigger deal.’ I want to be clear that this Oleshky thing is important
It really is aimed at a humanitarian ceasefire since there’s a lot of food that isn’t getting in, a lot of people are suffering and this potentially leads to some relief
But there are a lot of people around Ukraine and many bombed-out cities that are going, “Hey, what about us? We are hungry too

We don’t have certain services.”  Winter is coming, and the Russians have bombed out a lot of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, which is going to make this winter potentially very brutal, as a lot of folks will not have heating or the necessities they need to survive really cold temperatures
Steve Witkoff called Vladimir Putin a humanitarian, which had a lot of people shook because, famously, Vladimir Putin also started this war
Yeah, it’s like calling Freddy Krueger a nails enthusiast
Has Vladimir Putin released Americans that he took hostage? Yes
Has he returned some children that his government, his forces have taken? Yes
I don’t know if that makes a humanitarian
That’s kind of like praising the arsonist for throwing a bucket of water on the house fire

It’s not just calling him a humanitarian; it’s getting rid of the Lindsey Graham sanctions on Russia , which is essentially like handing Russia billions of dollars, right? There’s a lot of weirdness here

First of all, on the Graham bill, it’s a weird bill, and frankly it’s a pretty bad bill despite the fact that Democrats and Republicans love it.  What it basically calls for is tariffs on countries that purchase Russian energy

The way that Trump explains it is he waived the economic punishments, because otherwise the Russians would not have returned Stephen Hubbard and there might not have been this Oleshky ceasefire and there might not have been a bunch of other benefits

title: Patrick Stewart taught us what good men do with power
excerpt: Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. | CBS via Getty Images When Patrick Stewart, who died on Wednesday, first stepped onto the bridge of the Enterprise
body: Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. | CBS via Getty Images When Patrick Stewart, who died on Wednesday, first stepped onto the bridge of the Enterprise in 1987 in his defining role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, the Berlin Wall still stood
The Soviet Union would not fall until the fourth season of that show, Star Trek: The Next Generation, had already begun
Yet Picard’s generation of Star Trek franchise anticipated both events , portraying a post-Cold War world just as the Cold War was ending
It was the quintessential show for an age of American hegemony

For those unfamiliar with the franchise, Star Trek is primarily a story about Starfleet, which serves as both the military arm and as a kind of diplomatic corps for the United Federation of Planets, a benevolent, democratic union of more than a hundred worlds

In Star Trek’s Original Series, the 1960s episodes featuring Kirk and Spock, the Federation stands in the same shoes as the Cold War United States — vast and powerful, but also harried by other galactic superpowers like the Klingon Empire
Picard’s Federation, by contrast, is the sole dominant power in Earth’s quadrant of the galaxy

The Original Series’s writers conceived of the Klingons as thinly veiled stand-ins for the Soviet Union , but on Picard’s Enterprise there was a Klingon, Lieutenant Worf, serving directly behind Picard on the Enterprise’s bridge
Yet, while the Federation was a metaphor for an American empire victorious after the Cold War, it was also an idealized vision of the United States
The Enterprise spent far more time rescuing people from environmental catastrophes or shuttling ambassadors to peace negotiations than it did battling aliens in space
Picard flew around the galaxy in a ship packed with enough armaments to destroy entire planets
But he more often used that ship to distribute vaccines
In its best moments, The Next Generation was a meditation on the just use of power

And Picard, as Enterprise’s captain, was the voice of 1990s liberalism — known as much for his eloquent soliloquies in defense of universal rights as for his tactical prowess as commander of the Federation’s most advanced weapon
Looking back, it’s easy to see Picard’s liberalism as a vestige of a lost era
The Next Generation showcased a just and highly capable Federation that bears no resemblance whatsoever to the current United States government
But, while America has fallen far short of Star Trek’s Clinton-era aspirations, it would be a mistake to abandon those aspirations today
The children of nearly four decades ago watched Stewart’s portrayal of Picard and saw a role model for how the most powerful people in society should behave
Those lessons are just as relevant today as they were then
The institutionalist liberalism of Jean-Luc Picard The decision to cast Stewart, one of the preeminent Shakespearean actors of his generation , as the Enterprise’s captain was an inspired choice
Though the show often burdened its actors with heavy-handed dialogue, Stewart delivered his lines with the same aplomb and gravitas he would bring if he were playing Macbeth

Consider, for example, Stewart’s performance in The Measure of a Man , an early episode focused on the legal status of Lieutenant Commander Data, an android who serves as one of the Enterprise’s senior officers

In it, Data is ordered to report to an expert on artificial life forms who wishes to dismantle and study him in order to learn how to construct more, similar androids, and Picard is tasked with defending Data’s right to refuse this order before a judge that he personally loathes

The turning point in the episode comes when Picard realizes that he is arguing, not just to save one android’s life, but to prevent the creation of an entire class of people with no more rights than a toaster. “A single Data,” Picard says in the trial that will determine the android officer’s future, “is a curiosity, a wonder even
But thousands of Datas, isn’t that becoming a race?” “Are you prepared to condemn him and all who come after him to servitude and slavery?” Picard asks the judge in his closing argument
When this episode first aired in 1989, democracy was ascendant
The Berlin Wall would stand for only a few more months
And the United States had emerged from the 1960s and even escaped the Reagan administration with its commitment to civil rights intact

Just a few years earlier, American liberals outmaneuvered opponents of the landmark Voting Rights Act of 1965 — the law that probably did more than any other to dismantle Jim Crow — and persuaded President Ronald Reagan to sign legislation expanding its scope .  And so the conclusion of The Measure of a Man mirrors this optimistic reality
At the end of Picard’s courtroom defense of his android officer, the judge concludes that Data has the “freedom to choose” not to be dismantled and studied
In the liberal universe imagined by The Next Generation ’s writers, institutions are trustworthy and responsive to reasoned argument
Indeed, for a show about naval officers tasked with securing a hegemonic power, Star Trek spends a surprising amount of time on courtroom drama

In another episode, The Drumhead , Picard battles an admiral who is pulled out of retirement to investigate allegations of sabotage aboard the Enterprise — and who eventually leads a witch hunt into a largely innocent crewman whose only crime is hiding his Romulan ancestry (the Romulans, like the Original Series’s Klingons, are a longtime enemy of the Federation)

Like the trial of Commander Data, The Drumhead is best known for Picard’s speech in favor of universal rights. “When the first link of the chain is forged,” Picard tells the admiral, “the first speech censored, the first thought forbidden, the first freedom denied, it chains us all irrevocably.” And, in keeping with Star Trek’s belief that institutions can be forces of good, the episode ends with Starfleet’s head of security storming out of the admiral’s inquisition and putting an end to it

There have been several attempts to revive Star Trek during the Trump era, and they’ve often fallen flat in an age when US institutions can no longer be trusted to defend universal rights and freedoms

Star Trek: Discovery , which launched during Trump’s first year in office and aired for five seasons, featured sinister captains with hidden agendas, and culminated in two seasons about a collapsed, distrusted Federation struggling to rebuild itself

Indeed, when Stewart revisited his breakout role in Star Trek: Picard , an uneven series that opens with its titular character as a retired admiral, Picard is less a crusader for justice than a relic of a more enlightened age

In the series’s first episode, a reporter asks why he decided to resign from the Federation’s corps of warrior diplomats, and an angry Picard responds, “because it was no longer Starfleet!” He then denounces the Federation’s descent into prejudice against artificial life forms like Data, the very lives he fought to protect in The Measure of a Man
Picard might as well have been speaking about the United States
In 2020, when this episode first aired, the institutionalist liberalism that defined The Next Generation was hard to defend

title: Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.
excerpt: Eating disorders are surging globally: A new study in JAMA Psychiatry found anorexia and bulimia rose 71% between 1990 and 2023, affecting an estimated 18.1 mil
body: Eating disorders are surging globally: A new study in JAMA Psychiatry found anorexia and bulimia rose 71% between 1990 and 2023, affecting an estimated 18.1 million people—and experts say the true number affected by eating disorders is likely three times higher

Social media is fueling the crisis: TikTok's algorithm served users with eating disorders 4,343% more harmful content than those without—and clinicians say "thinspiration" trends can trigger new cases

GLP-1 drugs are making things worse: Experts are already seeing patients—some as young as 11—misusing weight-loss drugs " data-chronoton-post-id="1147838" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade
But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders
A new report suggests that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up between 1990 and 2023—by a whopping 71%
By 2023, there were an estimated 18.1 million people living with one of these two disorders
What’s worse is that the number is likely to be much higher than that once we factor in other eating disorders
And, disturbingly, those in the field are already starting to see GLP-1 weight-loss drugs exacerbating the issue
Cheri Levinson is a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville in Kentucky who has specialized in eating disorders for almost 20 years
She says she’s now seeing more patients with more severe symptoms than at any other time in her career, and that many of them are misusing GLP-1s. “This is the worst I’ve seen things,” she says
Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which people’s eating behaviors impact their health
They include anorexia nervosa (defined by a fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (in which people binge and purge), binge eating disorder, and others
It’s thought that some people have a genetic predisposition to certain eating disorders, but that some external factor is what triggers their onset
That might be stress, or social pressure to be skinny
Often, simply restricting food intake can trigger an eating disorder, says Levinson
Eating disorders—along with the pressure to look thin—were already prevalent in the 1990s (the  heroin chic era springs to mind)

To find out how things might have changed since then, Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China and his colleagues pulled together data from studies and surveys conducted on populations around the world
The team used statistical models to fill in any data gaps
That research allowed the researchers to estimate the annual incidence of two eating disorders—anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—for each of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023
They also estimated the impact those disorders had on global health by calculating their disability-adjusted life years (one  DALY represents a year of healthy life lost)
The findings, published in JAMA Psychiatry on Wednesday, are unsettling
Between 1990 and 2023, there was a 71% increase in the incidence of those two eating disorders, the team found
Those conditions had a huge impact on global health, too
In 2023, they “cost the world the equivalent of about 3.83 million years of healthy life,” says Bai
Bai and his colleagues expect these figures to continue to rise
In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people had either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa; by 2050, the team predict, the two conditions could affect 21.8 million people
Those two conditions represent less than half of all eating disorders, says Levinson, who was not involved in Bai’s study
The true impact of these disorders is “probably three times the rate that they’re reporting,” she says
Bai and his colleagues didn’t explore the reasons for this rise (although Bai points out that it can’t be entirely explained by population growth)

So how did we get here? Social media may have played a role. “Social media comparisons, influencers, challenges, diet trends can all be precipitating … events for an eating disorder,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, who was not involved in the new study
Bulik has been studying and treating eating disorders since the early 1980s. “Between 1990 and 2023 there has clearly been an upsurge of those types of environmental exposures,” she says

Many social media users are exposed to filtered and modified images of skinny influencers who may have undergone cosmetic surgery or extreme dieting and who are promoting “thinspiration” or “fitspiration” content
But users with eating disorders appear to be more likely to engage with this content—and to be fed more of it as a result

When researchers at the University of Melbourne  investigated this phenomenon a couple of years ago, they found that the algorithms of TikTok users with eating disorders delivered 4343% more “toxic eating disorder videos” than those of users who didn’t have the disorders
They also got more content focused on dieting or exercising
Many were fed over 1000 problematic videos per month
Bulik describes social media as “quicksand” for people with, or at risk of, eating disorders
The covid-19 pandemic—and the social isolation that accompanied lockdowns—also appears to have contributed to the rise in eating disorders
Research conducted in 2021 found that the number of people hospitalized with eating disorders in the US doubled between 2018 and 2020
Researchers don’t yet have good data on how trends in eating disorders might have progressed since 2023

title: Zombies are real – just ask the parasites taking over the bodies and brains of insects and rodents, leading them to their doom
url:
<title>Zombies are real – just ask the parasites taking over the bodies and brains of insects and rodents, leading them to their doom</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766774/original/file-20261016-50-crkhu4.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C136%2C2048%2C1365&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The fungus _Ophiocordyceps_ (stalk growing out of the ant&#39;s head) helped inspire the video game and show &quot;The Last of Us.&quot;</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.inaturalist.org/photos/407452035">Denis Zabin/iNaturalist</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Zombies have taken many forms in popular culture. In Michael Jackson’s “<a href="https://youtu.be/sOnqjkJTMaA">Thriller</a>” music video, corpses climb out of their graves and perform an impressively coordinated dance. In HBO’s “<a href="https://theconversation.com/pancakes-wont-turn-you-into-a-zombie-as-in-hbos-the-last-of-us-but-fungi-in-flour-have-been-making-people-sick-for-a-long-time-200428">The Last of Us</a>,” a fungus infects humans, takes over their bodies and turns them into hosts that help spread the infection. Even Plankton has tried his hand at taking control of another organism in “<a href="https://spongebob.fandom.com/wiki/Plankton!">SpongeBob SquarePants</a>.”</p>

<p>These examples are fictional, but they all play with the same unsettling idea: Can one organism take control of another, even after they’re dead? In nature, the answer is not quite as dramatic, but some parasites and fungi come surprisingly close. </p>

<p>I spend much of my time as a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Xe78w-wAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">biomedical engineer and synthetic biologist</a> thinking about how biological systems sense signals, process information and change their behavior. That is part of what makes the idea of one organism taking control of another so fascinating to me.</p>

<p>Some parasites and fungi can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.ento.54.110807.090556">alter the behavior of a living host</a> in ways that benefit the parasite. They do not bring the dead back to life. Instead, they interfere with biological systems that control movement, motivation and decision-making. </p>

<h2>Zombie ants and fungi</h2>

<p>The best-known example of a parasite changing its host’s behavior is the <a href="https://www.loc.gov/everyday-mysteries/categories/biology-and-human-anatomy/item/whats-up-with-zombie-ants/">“zombie ant” fungus</a>, <em>Ophiocordyceps</em>, which helped inspire “The Last of Us.”</p>

<p>The life cycle of the zombie ant fungus begins when fungal spores land on an ant. The spores stick to the ant’s outer surface and eventually break through it, allowing the fungus to enter the body. Once inside, the fungus grows and spreads while the ant is still alive. The infection can develop over several weeks before the most <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00253-024-13332-x">dramatic changes in the ant’s behavior</a> begin. </p>

<p>Eventually, the infected ant leaves the colony and begins wandering and climbing vegetation. This behavior moves the ant away from its normal habitat and into a location that favors fungal reproduction and dispersal. Near the end of the infection, the ant bites tightly onto a leaf, twig or other plant surface and remains attached in what researchers call a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00253-024-13332-x">death grip</a>. After the ant dies, the fungus consumes the remaining tissues and produces a stalk from the ant’s body. This structure releases spores that can fall on other ants below and begin the cycle again. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Dead ant biting the under" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=864&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=864&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=864&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1086&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1086&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1086&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">These ants show the characteristic death grip and head stalk of an <em>Ophiocordyceps</em> infection.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0004835">Pontoppidan et al/PLoS One</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>How does the fungus make the ant do this? You might imagine fungal cells invading the ant’s brain and taking control. Surprisingly, researchers examining infected ants before death found extensive fungal growth <a href="https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.200683">throughout the body and around muscle fibers</a>, but not inside the brain. Fungal cells can form networks around the ant’s muscles, suggesting that the ability to manipulate behavior may involve communication between the fungus and multiple host tissues rather than direct control of the brain.</p>

<p>The death grip provides an especially striking example of how the fungus can manipulate its host’s muscles. The jaw muscles of infected ants are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.200683">heavily colonized by the fungus</a>, showing signs of extreme contraction. There are also signs that the fungus may be releasing molecules near these tissues. Yet motor neurons and connections between nerves and muscles can remain intact. Together, these findings suggest that the fungus may alter the machinery controlling muscle contraction rather than simply destroying it. </p>

<p>Scientists still do not know exactly what causes ants to undergo the entire sequence of wandering, climbing and biting. While researchers have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00253-024-13332-x">identified fungal genes</a> associated with proteins, toxins and other compounds that could affect chemical signaling in the host, many of these possible mechanisms have not yet been proved. </p>

<p>That uncertainty is part of what makes the system so fascinating. The fungus does not appear to flip a single “zombie switch.” Instead, it may change several biological systems at once until the ant behaves in a way that benefits the fungus. </p>

<h2>How to create a zombie</h2>

<p><em>Ophiocordyceps</em> is not the only organism capable of changing a host’s behavior. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0010019">emerald jewel wasp, <em>Ampulex compressa</em></a>, uses a very different strategy: It injects venom into a cockroach’s nervous system. The cockroach is not paralyzed, but it becomes much less likely to start moving on its own or to escape. The wasp can then lead it to a burrow and lay an egg on it. </p>

<p>Researchers have shown that the venom reduces activity in parts of the nervous system involved in starting movement. In other words, the cockroach can still walk, but its drive to do so has been changed. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Wasp and cockroach head to head on a cement block" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">This cockroach takes its marching orders from the emerald jewel wasp.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vespa_Joia_arrastando_barata.jpg">JMGM/Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><a href="https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-a-parasitic-worm-forces-praying-mantises-to-drown-themselves/">Hairworms take behavioral manipulation</a> one step further by leading their hosts toward their own demise. Some species infect praying mantises or crickets and grow inside them while the insect is still alive. When the worm is ready to reproduce, the infected host becomes unusually attracted to light, which may draw it toward the shiny surface of water. The host enters the water, where the worm escapes from its body and begins the next stage of its life cycle. For the host that cannot swim, that behavior can be fatal.</p>

<p>Researchers are still working out exactly how the parasite causes this change, but studies have found changes in proteins in the host’s brain as the parasite manipulates it. In effect, the parasite appears to hijack the host’s sensory and behavioral machinery to guide it somewhere it would not normally go.  </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/YB6O7jS_VBM?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Unfortunately for crickets, hairworms also find them good hosts.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Behavioral manipulation also occurs in mammals. <a href="https://theconversation.com/toxoplasma-is-a-common-parasite-that-causes-birth-defects-but-the-us-doesnt-screen-for-it-during-pregnancy-232936"><em>Toxoplasma gondii</em></a> can infect many warm-blooded animals, but it reproduces in cats. </p>

<p>While rodents normally avoid cat odors, those infected with the parasite can lose some of that natural aversion and even <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0608310104">become attracted to cat odors</a>. This change could increase the chance that an infected rodent is eaten by a cat, allowing the parasite to complete its life cycle.</p>

<h2>More than mind control</h2>

<p>These examples show why “mind control” is an imperfect description of how parasites manipulate their hosts. Parasites do not need to control every action that their host makes. They may only need to change one key behavior: whether to climb, whether to walk away, whether to enter water or whether to avoid a predator. </p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Microscopy image of an oblong blob with smaller circles within" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption"><em>Toxoplasma gondii</em> cycle between rodents, cats and humans.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Toxoplasma_gondii_(2).jpg">AJ Cann/Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>There is no single “zombie switch.” Behavior emerges from communication between the nervous system, muscles and other tissues throughout the body. Different parasites have evolved different ways to interfere with those systems.</p>

<p>So biology cannot create the dancing dead of “Thriller” or the infected humans of “The Last of Us.” But if a zombie is a living organism whose normal behavior has been redirected by another organism, nature has already created plenty of them. </p>

<p>Studying these real-life zombies may help scientists understand not only how parasites manipulate their hosts, but also how normal behavior is generated and controlled in the first place.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292955/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <summary>Parasitic fungi, wasps, worms and amoeba can control the behavior of their hosts in various horrifying ways.</summary>

body: The fungus _Ophiocordyceps_ (stalk growing out of the ant's head) helped inspire the video game and show "The Last of Us." Denis Zabin/iNaturalist , CC BY-SA Zombies have taken many forms in popular culture
In Michael Jackson’s “ Thriller ” music video, corpses climb out of their graves and perform an impressively coordinated dance
In HBO’s “ The Last of Us ,” a fungus infects humans, takes over their bodies and turns them into hosts that help spread the infection

Even Plankton has tried his hand at taking control of another organism in “ SpongeBob SquarePants .” These examples are fictional, but they all play with the same unsettling idea: Can one organism take control of another, even after they’re dead? In nature, the answer is not quite as dramatic, but some parasites and fungi come surprisingly close
I spend much of my time as a biomedical engineer and synthetic biologist thinking about how biological systems sense signals, process information and change their behavior
That is part of what makes the idea of one organism taking control of another so fascinating to me
Some parasites and fungi can alter the behavior of a living host in ways that benefit the parasite
Instead, they interfere with biological systems that control movement, motivation and decision-making

Zombie ants and fungi The best-known example of a parasite changing its host’s behavior is the “zombie ant” fungus , Ophiocordyceps , which helped inspire “The Last of Us.” The life cycle of the zombie ant fungus begins when fungal spores land on an ant
The spores stick to the ant’s outer surface and eventually break through it, allowing the fungus to enter the body
Once inside, the fungus grows and spreads while the ant is still alive
The infection can develop over several weeks before the most dramatic changes in the ant’s behavior begin
Eventually, the infected ant leaves the colony and begins wandering and climbing vegetation
This behavior moves the ant away from its normal habitat and into a location that favors fungal reproduction and dispersal
Near the end of the infection, the ant bites tightly onto a leaf, twig or other plant surface and remains attached in what researchers call a death grip
After the ant dies, the fungus consumes the remaining tissues and produces a stalk from the ant’s body
This structure releases spores that can fall on other ants below and begin the cycle again
These ants show the characteristic death grip and head stalk of an Ophiocordyceps infection
Pontoppidan et al/PLoS One , CC BY-SA How does the fungus make the ant do this? You might imagine fungal cells invading the ant’s brain and taking control
Surprisingly, researchers examining infected ants before death found extensive fungal growth throughout the body and around muscle fibers , but not inside the brain

Fungal cells can form networks around the ant’s muscles, suggesting that the ability to manipulate behavior may involve communication between the fungus and multiple host tissues rather than direct control of the brain
The death grip provides an especially striking example of how the fungus can manipulate its host’s muscles
The jaw muscles of infected ants are heavily colonized by the fungus , showing signs of extreme contraction
There are also signs that the fungus may be releasing molecules near these tissues
Yet motor neurons and connections between nerves and muscles can remain intact
Together, these findings suggest that the fungus may alter the machinery controlling muscle contraction rather than simply destroying it
Scientists still do not know exactly what causes ants to undergo the entire sequence of wandering, climbing and biting

While researchers have identified fungal genes associated with proteins, toxins and other compounds that could affect chemical signaling in the host, many of these possible mechanisms have not yet been proved
That uncertainty is part of what makes the system so fascinating
The fungus does not appear to flip a single “zombie switch.” Instead, it may change several biological systems at once until the ant behaves in a way that benefits the fungus
How to create a zombie Ophiocordyceps is not the only organism capable of changing a host’s behavior
The emerald jewel wasp, Ampulex compressa , uses a very different strategy: It injects venom into a cockroach’s nervous system
The cockroach is not paralyzed, but it becomes much less likely to start moving on its own or to escape
The wasp can then lead it to a burrow and lay an egg on it
Researchers have shown that the venom reduces activity in parts of the nervous system involved in starting movement
In other words, the cockroach can still walk, but its drive to do so has been changed
This cockroach takes its marching orders from the emerald jewel wasp
JMGM/Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA Hairworms take behavioral manipulation one step further by leading their hosts toward their own demise
Some species infect praying mantises or crickets and grow inside them while the insect is still alive
When the worm is ready to reproduce, the infected host becomes unusually attracted to light, which may draw it toward the shiny surface of water

title: From 18th-century false ballots to the second JFK and double Dan Sullivans, a brief history of spoiler candidates and the unsuccessful legal challenges to them

<title>From 18th-century false ballots to the second JFK and double Dan Sullivans, a brief history of spoiler candidates and the unsuccessful legal challenges to them</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769277/original/file-20261030-64-20ykxi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C4363%2C2908&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The campaign of U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola of Alaska, a Democrat, has been rocked by accusations it recruited a spoiler candidate for the ballot.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Election2026AlaskaSenate/7c677439d102421cab070adee77bd35a/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=Peltola&amp;currentItemNo=2&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP/Mark Thiessen</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Less than a week before Election Day, The New York Times <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/us/politics/alaska-dan-sullivan-conspiracy-peltola.html">reported</a> that people with links to Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s U.S. Senate campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had recruited a candidate to the race whose name is nearly identical to that of the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, whom Peltola was challenging. The plan aimed to siphon votes from the incumbent senator and help Peltola win, according to the reporting.</p>

<p>The story has driven calls for <a href="https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/10/28/trump-calls-for-peltola-to-be-criminally-charged-removed-from-alaskas-u-s-senate-race/">prosecutions</a>, lawsuits and <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/alaskas-governor-orders-a-probe-into-peltolas-senate-campaign-over-spoiler-candidate-controversy">state action</a>. But <a href="https://www.coastal.edu/academics/facultyprofiles/educationandsocialsciences/politics/drewkurlowski/">as a political scientist who studies election law</a>, I can say that the spoiler candidate is one of the oldest tricks in the American campaign toolbox, and the law has rarely touched it.</p>

<h2>Early ballots</h2>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769284/original/file-20261030-64-xpfkya.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A yellowed ballot with 'FREE SOIL ELECTORAL TICKET' and a farmer driving a horse-drawn plow." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769284/original/file-20261030-64-xpfkya.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769284/original/file-20261030-64-xpfkya.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=837&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769284/original/file-20261030-64-xpfkya.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=837&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769284/original/file-20261030-64-xpfkya.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=837&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769284/original/file-20261030-64-xpfkya.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1052&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769284/original/file-20261030-64-xpfkya.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1052&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769284/original/file-20261030-64-xpfkya.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1052&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">19th-century voting usually involved casting a ballot printed by political parties, such as this electoral ticket for the Free Soil Party from 1848.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.si.edu/es/object/free-soil-electoral-ticket-1836%3Anmah_529060">Smithsonian National Museum of American History</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>For most of the 1800s, American elections were conducted with ballots designed and printed by the parties. There were no official ballots printed by the state. </p>

<p>In those days, the addition of a rival name to a party ballot by an insidious printer could swing countless votes to the opposing party. The tactic was well known, and voters were often warned to look out for the “<a href="https://www.americanheritage.com/magic-ballot">Spurious Ticket</a>.”</p>

<p>By the 1890s, the government-printed ballot had gained widespread adoption and ended the practice of counterfeit tickets. But that would not be enough to deter those who wanted to deceive voters.</p>

<h2>Power of a name</h2>

<p>As <a href="https://www.adn.com/opinions/2026/07/05/opinion-the-two-joseph-russos-are-as-relatable-as-two-dan-sullivans/">observers in Alaska have noted</a>, recruiting candidates with similar or identical names is not a new move. </p>

<p>In John F. Kennedy’s first congressional primary, his opponent was a city councilor named Joseph Russo. An aide to Kennedy <a href="https://thewestendmuseum.org/history/era/immigrant-neighborhood/jfk-and-the-two-joe-russos/">reportedly paid a janitor</a> with the same name to enter the race. The real Russo complained, but in the end, Kennedy took more votes in the 1946 race than the Russos combined.</p>

<p>Eight years later, the name Kennedy worked the other way, when a <a href="https://commonwealthbeacon.org/politics/all-about-the-iotheri-other-jfk/">Gillette stockroom supervisor named John Francis Kennedy</a>, no relation, was elected as a Democrat to the position of treasurer and receiver-general of Massachusetts, owing in large part to the familiarity of his name. Names can move votes, so namesakes can be worth recruiting.</p>

<h2>Spoilers as surrogates</h2>

<p>Some spoiler candidates are not necessarily meant to win votes. Sometimes they are there to amplify a message. </p>

<p>In 1978, Republican Carroll Campbell was <a href="https://www.scencyclopedia.org/sce/entries/campbell-carroll-ashmore-jr/">running for an open House seat</a> in upstate South Carolina. His opponent was <a href="https://forward.com/culture/205485/when-greenville-south-carolina-had-a-jewish-mayor/">Max Heller, the mayor of Greenville</a> and a Jewish refugee from Nazi-occupied Austria.</p>

<p>Days before the election, Don Sprouse, an independent running for office for the first time, <a href="https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/atwater/etc/script.html">held a press conference</a> and <a href="https://scholarexchange.furman.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1075&amp;context=fhr">declared that Heller was unfit</a> for office as he had “not made clear to the voters he is not a Christian” and was “not as qualified to represent the Christian people.” </p>

<p>Although Campbell condemned the remarks and Sprouse received only 1,693 votes, Heller lost the race. The allegations, still unproven, of Sprouse <a href="https://scholarexchange.furman.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1075&amp;context=fhr">being a “stalking-horse”</a> for Campbell only surfaced years later, but they <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1986/09/17/haunted-by-1978-speech/906ab861-dd65-4d61-a4a0-7a68dbc6e566/">continued to dog Campbell</a> when he ran for governor in 1986.</p>

<p>Sprouse wasn’t going to spoil the election with the votes he could win, but he could be a spoiler with his message, an antisemitic appeal that Campbell would not make directly.  </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769280/original/file-20261030-78-o526cw.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A clipping from the New York Times with the headline 'Bigotry Issue in Carolina Campaign.'" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769280/original/file-20261030-78-o526cw.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769280/original/file-20261030-78-o526cw.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769280/original/file-20261030-78-o526cw.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769280/original/file-20261030-78-o526cw.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769280/original/file-20261030-78-o526cw.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=510&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769280/original/file-20261030-78-o526cw.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=510&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769280/original/file-20261030-78-o526cw.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=510&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A spoiler candidate who made antisemitic remarks in a 1978 South Carolina campaign for the House of Representatives became a campaign issue eight years later.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.nytimes.com/1986/09/24/us/bigotry-issue-in-carolina-campaign.html">New York Times archive</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Candidates who don’t even know they’re running</h2>

<p>A different type of ballot shenanigan skips the recruitment and simply puts candidates on the ballot. </p>

<p>This was the case in 2010 when two Oakland County, Michigan, Democratic officials put candidates on the ballot <a href="https://talkingpointsmemo.com/muckraker/michigan-dem-pleads-no-contest-in-fake-tea-party-scheme">under the Tea Party label</a> in three races. The candidates didn’t even know they were running.</p>

<p>In this case, the law did come back to bite. The county party chair and operations director were <a href="https://www.salon.com/2011/03/17/dems_tea_party_charges/">charged with perjury and forgery</a>, but the crime was forging signatures, not their strategy. </p>

<p>Some state election codes specifically discuss false declarations or forged election paperwork, but many don’t contemplate this type of scheme. Forgery and perjury, however, are illegal across the country, and it’s almost impossible to put an unwitting person on the ballot without one or the other.</p>

<h2>Alaska: No barriers</h2>

<p>In Alaska, this tactic can be used cheaply. There is no petition requirement to get on the ballot, just a $100 fee. Moreover, the parties can’t vet candidates in the primary. <a href="https://www.elections.alaska.gov/election-information/">The state’s unique top-four primary system</a> lets candidates choose their own party label.</p>

<p>The saga of <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Daniel_J._Sullivan_Jr._(Alaska_U.S._Senate_candidate)">Daniel J. Sullivan</a>, the schoolteacher known as <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOM9VeHndHQ">“Petersburg Sullivan” because of where he lives</a>, and <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Dan_S._Sullivan_(United_States_Senator_from_Alaska)">Sen. Dan S. Sullivan</a> goes back longer than recent revelations. </p>

<p>Petersburg Sullivan filed to run as a Republican in the Senate race just three days before the deadline; state officials tried to bar him from the ballot. In June <a href="https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/alaska-judge-puts-other-dan-sullivan-back-us-senate-ballot-2026-06-27/">a judge said</a> there was nothing in Alaska law to prevent him from appearing on the ballot, and <a href="https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/06/29/alaska-supreme-court-rules-dan-j-sullivan-eligible-to-run-for-us-senate/">the state Supreme Court subsequently agreed.</a></p>

<p>Since he couldn’t be removed, the state Division of Elections took unusual steps on their ballot design to help distinguish the two candidates. They listed Sen. Dan S. Sullivan as a Republican, marking him as the incumbent, and <a href="https://www.newsweek.com/odds-dan-sullivans-advancing-alaska-senate-race-court-ruling-12145780">left Daniel J. Sullivan without a party designation</a>. This had not been done for previous incumbents in at least a decade.</p>

<h2>What the law can do</h2>

<p>Assuming there is no forgery of documents with an unwitting and unwilling spoiler candidate, there is little the law can do. History shows us that the real legal exposure in these cases usually lies where it most often does in politics: money. </p>

<p>In a 2020 Miami, Florida, race, a former state senator turned political operative was <a href="https://www.nbcmiami.com/news/local/ex-florida-senator-frank-artiles-to-be-sentenced-in-ghost-candidate-scheme/3450503/">convicted of three felonies</a> related to efforts to recruit and pay a decoy candidate with the same surname as the Democratic incumbent. In another Florida case, a local Republican Party chair was convicted in connection with a <a href="https://wusf.org/politics-issues/2022-09-02/seminole-county-gop-chair-guilty-ghost-candidate-scheme">scheme to plant a progressive alternative</a> to siphon votes from the Democratic candidate. In both cases the prosecutions focused on campaign finance crimes, not simply on putting the spoilers on the ballot.</p>

<p>The state of Washington is an outlier, where it is <a href="https://www.foxnews.com/media/washington-governors-race-loses-two-bob-fergusons-attorney-general-bob-ferguson-issues-legal-threats">a felony to run under a rival’s surname if the intent is to confuse voters</a>. In 2024, two Bob Fergusons were recruited by conservative activist Glen Morgan to run for governor against state Attorney General Bob Ferguson. Both opted to drop out of their race under threat of prosecution.</p>

<p>There is nothing comparable to these laws in Alaska, however, and whether laws like this could prevent this type of thing in a federal election is still untested. Under the Supreme Court’s decision in <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/1994/93-1456">U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton</a> in 1995, states cannot add their own qualifications for Congress.</p>

<h2>Read your ballots!</h2>

<p><a href="https://hd.housedivided.dickinson.edu/node/33602">The advice</a> from 1860 – “Watch your tickets on election day. There’s a scheme on foot …” – when <a href="https://hd.housedivided.dickinson.edu/node/33599">newspapers urged voters</a> to read their tickets before casting their vote, is still relevant long after the demise of the party ticket. It is unlikely that the law can solve this problem, because to do so would be to wade into the First Amendment waters of why people run for office. Regulating thought and intention is a dangerous proposition under the Constitution.</p>

<p>The old answer is the best one. Self-government depends less on clever rules and more on citizens paying attention. Read your ballots!</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295504/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
