body: Senate candidate Mary Peltola of Alaska, a Democrat, has been rocked by accusations it recruited a spoiler candidate for the ballot
AP/Mark Thiessen Less than a week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that people with links to Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s U.S

Senate campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had recruited a candidate to the race whose name is nearly identical to that of the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, whom Peltola was challenging
The plan aimed to siphon votes from the incumbent senator and help Peltola win, according to the reporting
The story has driven calls for prosecutions , lawsuits and state action
But as a political scientist who studies election law , I can say that the spoiler candidate is one of the oldest tricks in the American campaign toolbox, and the law has rarely touched it
Early ballots 19th-century voting usually involved casting a ballot printed by political parties, such as this electoral ticket for the Free Soil Party from 1848
Smithsonian National Museum of American History For most of the 1800s, American elections were conducted with ballots designed and printed by the parties
There were no official ballots printed by the state
In those days, the addition of a rival name to a party ballot by an insidious printer could swing countless votes to the opposing party

The tactic was well known, and voters were often warned to look out for the “ Spurious Ticket .” By the 1890s, the government-printed ballot had gained widespread adoption and ended the practice of counterfeit tickets
But that would not be enough to deter those who wanted to deceive voters
Power of a name As observers in Alaska have noted , recruiting candidates with similar or identical names is not a new move
Kennedy’s first congressional primary, his opponent was a city councilor named Joseph Russo
An aide to Kennedy reportedly paid a janitor with the same name to enter the race
The real Russo complained, but in the end, Kennedy took more votes in the 1946 race than the Russos combined

Eight years later, the name Kennedy worked the other way, when a Gillette stockroom supervisor named John Francis Kennedy , no relation, was elected as a Democrat to the position of treasurer and receiver-general of Massachusetts, owing in large part to the familiarity of his name
Names can move votes, so namesakes can be worth recruiting
Spoilers as surrogates Some spoiler candidates are not necessarily meant to win votes
Sometimes they are there to amplify a message
In 1978, Republican Carroll Campbell was running for an open House seat in upstate South Carolina
His opponent was Max Heller, the mayor of Greenville and a Jewish refugee from Nazi-occupied Austria

Days before the election, Don Sprouse, an independent running for office for the first time, held a press conference and declared that Heller was unfit for office as he had “not made clear to the voters he is not a Christian” and was “not as qualified to represent the Christian people.” Although Campbell condemned the remarks and Sprouse received only 1,693 votes, Heller lost the race
The allegations, still unproven, of Sprouse being a “stalking-horse” for Campbell only surfaced years later, but they continued to dog Campbell when he ran for governor in 1986
Sprouse wasn’t going to spoil the election with the votes he could win, but he could be a spoiler with his message, an antisemitic appeal that Campbell would not make directly
A spoiler candidate who made antisemitic remarks in a 1978 South Carolina campaign for the House of Representatives became a campaign issue eight years later
New York Times archive Candidates who don’t even know they’re running A different type of ballot shenanigan skips the recruitment and simply puts candidates on the ballot
This was the case in 2010 when two Oakland County, Michigan, Democratic officials put candidates on the ballot under the Tea Party label in three races
The candidates didn’t even know they were running
In this case, the law did come back to bite
The county party chair and operations director were charged with perjury and forgery , but the crime was forging signatures, not their strategy
Some state election codes specifically discuss false declarations or forged election paperwork, but many don’t contemplate this type of scheme
Forgery and perjury, however, are illegal across the country, and it’s almost impossible to put an unwitting person on the ballot without one or the other
Alaska: No barriers In Alaska, this tactic can be used cheaply
There is no petition requirement to get on the ballot, just a $100 fee
Moreover, the parties can’t vet candidates in the primary
The state’s unique top-four primary system lets candidates choose their own party label
Sullivan , the schoolteacher known as “Petersburg Sullivan” because of where he lives , and Sen
Sullivan goes back longer than recent revelations
Petersburg Sullivan filed to run as a Republican in the Senate race just three days before the deadline; state officials tried to bar him from the ballot

<title>Allegheny County is reassessing every property – here’s how your tax bill is calculated now</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768300/original/file-20261026-52-ttafk2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C2%2C2118%2C1412&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A court-ordered reassessment will set new values for every property in Allegheny County.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/close-quarters-royalty-free-image/174187913?phrase=pittsburgh%20homes&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Robert D. Strovers/Moments Collection via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Allegheny County will undergo a countywide <a href="https://www.alleghenycounty.us/News-Articles/Allegheny-County-Press-Releases/August-2026-PR/08-17-2026-Countywide-Reassessment">reassessment of every property it taxes</a> for the first time since 2012. A county judge ordered the reassessment in August 2026, requiring the work to begin by July 1, 2027, and finish <a href="https://www.wesanews.org/politics-government/2026-08-17/allegheny-county-property-reassessment-2027-court-order">within five years</a>.</p>

<p>The goal is to bring property values in line with today’s market. That could shift the tax burden among property owners across the county. State <a href="https://www.alleghenyinstitute.org/penn-hills-will-test-assessment-law/">anti-windfall rules</a> may require local governments to lower their tax rates after a reassessment to ensure they balance and equalize the tax reassessments. Individual bills may go up or down.</p>

<p>For many homeowners, property taxes are confusing. Terms such as <a href="https://whyy.org/articles/what-is-a-millage-rate-and-how-does-it-affect-school-funding/">assessment, millage rate and school district tax</a> come up often, but taxpayers may not know what they mean or how each one affects their annual tax bill.</p>

<p>In Pittsburgh, property taxes pay for schools, parks, libraries, public safety and other local services. </p>

<p>I research and teach government finance at <a href="https://harrisburg.psu.edu/faculty-and-staff/elizabeth-jane-beckett-camarata">Penn State Harrisburg</a>, including a course on state and local taxation. Here’s a plain-language guide to how Pittsburgh’s property taxes work.</p>

<h2>What your home is worth – on paper</h2>

<p>The first concept is the property assessment. Allegheny County’s Office of Property Assessments gives every property an assessed value. That value is the basis for calculating property taxes.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768302/original/file-20261026-52-fxf9dv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An old building juxtaposed against modern skyscrapers." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768302/original/file-20261026-52-fxf9dv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768302/original/file-20261026-52-fxf9dv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768302/original/file-20261026-52-fxf9dv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768302/original/file-20261026-52-fxf9dv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768302/original/file-20261026-52-fxf9dv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768302/original/file-20261026-52-fxf9dv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768302/original/file-20261026-52-fxf9dv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The Allegheny County Courthouse is also home to the county treasurer’s office, which collects county property taxes.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/pittsburgh-royalty-free-image/487053147?phrase=allegheny%20county%20courthouse&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">tupungato/iStock Collection via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>An assessed value isn’t necessarily what a home would sell for today. Some places, such as <a href="https://www.phila.gov/departments/board-of-revision-of-taxes/faq">Philadelphia</a>, assess property at full market value. Other jurisdictions assess property at a set percentage of market value. In <a href="https://www.cookcountyassessoril.gov/how-residential-property-valued-0">Cook County, Illinois</a>, which includes Chicago, homes are assessed at 10% of their market value. That doesn’t mean Chicago-area homeowners pay less. When assessments are a smaller share of market value, tax rates are set higher to raise the same amount of money. Allegheny County assesses at full value, but it uses what properties were worth in 2012. The court-ordered reassessment is meant to close the gap between those 2012 values and today’s market.</p>

<p>Allegheny County’s 14-year gap would be unusual almost anywhere else. Pennsylvania is the only state that doesn’t require counties to reassess on a regular schedule, while most states do so at least every six years. Within Pennsylvania, though, Allegheny is far from the worst: Butler County hasn’t reassessed <a href="https://www.axios.com/local/pittsburgh/2026/08/17/allegheny-county-reassess-585000-properties">since 1969</a>.</p>

<p>Homeowners can look up their assessment on the <a href="https://realestate.alleghenycounty.us">county’s real estate portal</a>.</p>

<h2>What a mill means</h2>

<p>Once a property has an assessed value, each local government applies a millage rate to figure out the tax owed. One mill equals $1 of tax for every $1,000 of assessed value. A home assessed at $100,000 has 100 units of $1,000 in value. </p>

<p>Pittsburgh property owners pay property taxes to three government entities: Allegheny County, the City of Pittsburgh and Pittsburgh Public Schools. Each one <a href="https://pghpropertytax.org/FAQ.pdf">sets its own millage rate</a>.</p>

<p>For 2026, the city’s general rate is 9.67 mills. The city also charges 0.5 mill for parks and 0.25 mill for libraries. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, and Allegheny County charges 6.43 mills. </p>

<p>Together, those rates add up to 27.307 mills. For a city home assessed at $100,000, that comes to about $2,731 a year before any exemptions or discounts.  </p>

<p>The county’s <a href="https://alleghenycontroller.com/property-tax-estimate/">property tax worksheet</a> and the <a href="https://alleghenycountytreasurer.us/real-estate-tax">county treasurer’s millage rate page</a> list current rates. These rates are set each year, and all of them will be cut when reassessed values take effect, since the law requires rates to drop as total values rise. </p>

<h2>The biggest slice: Schools</h2>

<p>School taxes are often the largest share of a homeowner’s property tax bill. In Pennsylvania, property taxes are a major <a href="https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/11/pennsylvania-budget-public-school-funding-tax-burden-adequacy-gaps-education/">source of revenue for public schools</a>. They help fund salaries for teachers, updates and maintainance for buildings, transportation, and technology and educational programs. </p>



<p>School tax rates vary widely across Allegheny County. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, well below the suburban districts around it. <a href="https://www.northallegheny.org/page/176">North Allegheny</a>, one of the lowest-taxing suburban districts, charges about 20.4 mills for the 2026-27 school year. Two of the highest are <a href="https://apps.alleghenycounty.us/website/muniprofile.asp?muni=73">Mt. Lebanon</a> at about 32 mills and <a href="https://apps.alleghenycounty.us/website/MuniProfile.asp?muni=85">Penn Hills</a> at about 32.6 mills. The county treasurer publishes a <a href="https://alleghenycountytreasurer.us/real-estate-tax">full list of school district rates</a>.</p>

<h2>Help for homeowners and seniors</h2>

<p>Some homeowners qualify for programs that lower their tax bills.</p>

<p>The Allegheny County Homestead exemption, <a href="https://www.alleghenycounty.us/Services/Property-Assessments-and-Real-Estate/Tax-Abatements-and-Exemptions/HomesteadFarmstead-Exclusion-Act-50">known as Act 50</a>, cuts $18,000 from the assessed value of a qualified, owner-occupied, primary residence property’s county taxes. There’s no income limit: Any homeowner who lives in the property as their primary residence qualifies. A home assessed at $100,000 is taxed on just $82,000, which saves about $116 a year. Enrolling in Act 50 also automatically applies <a href="https://www.pittsburghpa.gov/City-Government/Finance-Budget/Taxes/Tax-Relief-and-Assistance-Resources">Pittsburgh’s $15,000 exemption</a>, which covers the parks and library levies, and a larger Pittsburgh Public Schools exemption that is set each year. Applications for this exemption are due March 1 and need to be filed only once.</p>

<p>The senior citizen tax relief program, <a href="https://www.alleghenycounty.us/real-estate/abatements-exemptions/index.aspx">known as Act 77</a>, takes another 30% off county taxes for homeowners who are at least 60, have household incomes of $30,000 or less and have owned and lived in their home for at least 10 years. For a qualifying senior with that $100,000 home, the county bill would drop from about $527 to about $369.</p>

<h2>If you think your assessment’s too high</h2>

<p>Homeowners who believe their assessment is too high can appeal their assessment to the county’s <a href="https://www.alleghenycounty.us/Services/Property-Assessments-and-Real-Estate/Appeals/Board-of-Property-Assessment-Appeals-and-Review-BPAAR">Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review</a>. Filing is free; appeals can be submitted online, by email or in person.</p>

<p>Appeals are filed the year before the tax year they affect. The appeal window for 2027 bills closed Sept. 1, 2026. The next window, for 2028 bills, is expected to run from July 1 to Sept. 1, 2027, around the time the reassessment is set to begin.</p>

<p>At an appeal hearing, homeowners can argue their property’s value using either 2012 prices or today’s market. Recent sales of similar homes nearby can help show whether an assessment is out of line. The board can lower the assessment, leave it as is or raise it. </p>

<h2>What reassessment means for you</h2>

<p>Pittsburgh property taxes come down to two elements: the property’s assessed value and the millage rates set by the county, the city and the school district. Understanding how these elements work together can help homeowners read and comprehend their tax bills and better plan for one of the biggest ongoing costs of owning a home, next to the mortgage payment.</p>

<p>That understanding will matter more as the reassessment gets underway. When new values take effect, some homeowners will see their share of the tax burden rise and others will see it fall. The direction depends on how their property’s value has changed compared with changes of other similar properties since 2012.</p>

<title>Why achieving your goals can leave you feeling so empty</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768630/original/file-20261027-52-c3vlu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2239%2C1492&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Pleasure lies not just in getting what you want, but in the longing that propels you toward it.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/carefree-woman-with-lots-of-hot-air-ballons-royalty-free-image/503568493?phrase=reaching%20for%20balloon%20illustration&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">gremlin/iStock via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>When Anne Carson learned she had won the Nobel Prize in literature, she was in Iceland, where, <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/educational/nobel-prize-lessons/text-for-students-literature-2026/">according to the Swedish Academy</a>, she was “listening to the wind.”</p>

<p>Carson didn’t answer her phone right away, silencing it until her husband persuaded her to <a href="https://youtu.be/9_KWkHyvVfM?si=dB9epEhAHbZ5a7zl">call back</a>. Her verdict on the academy’s choice: “I think you’re all insane.”</p>

<p>Whatever she felt in the moment, there is an irony in Carson’s Nobel win. The highest award in literature has gone to a writer who has spent her career exploring the emptiness of a desire fulfilled. </p>

<p>The honor coincides with the 40th anniversary of the publication of her first book, “<a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691250625/eros-the-bittersweet">Eros the Bittersweet</a>,” a meditation on desire. </p>

<p>In it, Carson argues that desire begins with a void – with wanting what we don’t have. She traces how this feeling of absence shapes love, reading, writing and thinking, activities that renew themselves precisely because they are never complete. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768633/original/file-20261027-52-ccjy17.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A table featuring an array of books propped up on book stands." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768633/original/file-20261027-52-ccjy17.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768633/original/file-20261027-52-ccjy17.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=437&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768633/original/file-20261027-52-ccjy17.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=437&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768633/original/file-20261027-52-ccjy17.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=437&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768633/original/file-20261027-52-ccjy17.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=550&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768633/original/file-20261027-52-ccjy17.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=550&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768633/original/file-20261027-52-ccjy17.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=550&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Books by Canadian writer and poet Anne Carson – including ‘Eros: The Bittersweet’ – are displayed during a press conference announcing the winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature at the Swedish Academy in Stockholm, Sweden, on Oct. 8, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/books-by-canadian-writer-and-poet-anne-carson-are-displayed-news-photo/2298575212?phrase=anne%20carson&amp;adppopup=true">Atila Altuntas/Anadolu via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The philosopher and the top</h2>

<p>“Eros” begins with a brief preface on Franz Kafka’s “<a href="https://biblioklept.org/2014/08/04/the-top-franz-kafka/">The Top</a>,” a story about a philosopher who spends his time around children so he can chase their spinning tops. When a child sets a top in motion, the philosopher snatches it, believing that understanding any small thing, even a spinning top, would be enough to understand everything. </p>

<p>While the top spins, the philosopher is filled with hope, but as soon as he grasps it, he is repelled by the dumb piece of wood. He throws it down and waits for the next child to spin a top.</p>

<p>For Carson, the story is about why people love to fall in love. <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691250625/eros-the-bittersweet">The philosopher is after what Carson calls</a> an “impertinent stability in vertigo,” a state that is “itself delightful, a suspended moment of living hope.” The philosopher’s quest for knowledge, Carson cheekily concludes, is simply his pretext for chasing spinning tops. He is enchanted by the spinning itself, and even by his own enchantment – a spell that breaks the instant the top stops in his hand.</p>

<p>Most people know a version of this: There is something animating about chasing a goal. But once attained, the framed degree fades into the wall, the promotion quickly loses its luster, and the plaque becomes another dumb piece of wood. </p>

<p>The delight of wanting disappears in the having. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A rainbow-colored wooden top spinning." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768631/original/file-20261027-52-j5xi00.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768631/original/file-20261027-52-j5xi00.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=340&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768631/original/file-20261027-52-j5xi00.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=340&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768631/original/file-20261027-52-j5xi00.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=340&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768631/original/file-20261027-52-j5xi00.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=427&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768631/original/file-20261027-52-j5xi00.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=427&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768631/original/file-20261027-52-j5xi00.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=427&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

<h2>A hole in the self</h2>

<p>Why does fulfillment so often feel like loss? </p>

<p>Carson’s answer begins with the Greek word for erotic love, “eros,” which she explains denotes want or lack. Plato’s Socrates makes the same point in the “<a href="https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/1600/pg1600-images.html">Symposium</a>.” For the Greeks, no one desires what they already have. </p>

<p>Desire also opens up an absence. To long for someone or something is to discover our own edges, the chasm where the self ends and what is wanted begins. Eros reveals that we are incomplete – an awareness that causes the self to become undone, loosening at the joints.   </p>

<p>In one of her poems, the Greek poet Sappho called this experience “<a href="https://westbraeliterarygroup.com/sappho-poems/fragment-130">glukupikron</a>,” or “sweetbitter.” </p>

<p><a href="https://www.commonwealmagazine.org/sweetbitter">Carson’s translation of the passage reads</a>: “Eros once again limb-loosener whirls me / sweetbitter, impossible to fight off, creature stealing up.” </p>

<p>Sappho puts sweet first, Carson notes in “Eros,” but desire is not initially sweet and then bitter. Pleasure and pain arrive together, in the same body and at the same time, before the lover is even able to distinguish them. </p>

<p>Carson extends this pattern to reading, writing and thinking. A reader approaches a text’s meaning but never masters it; every rereading turns up new meanings. The pleasure of understanding and the ache of incompleteness arrive together. </p>

<p>Writing works the same way. A good sentence both captures and conceals what the writer means. Thinking also runs on that doubled feeling, which is how the story of a philosopher chasing tops ended up in a book about love. </p>

<h2>The trouble with goals</h2>

<p>The same bittersweet pattern also shows up somewhere far less romantic: at work. Meeting a deadline brings relief that is already hollow because the next one is waiting. </p>

<p>I discovered “Eros the Bittersweet” as a philosophy graduate student, when my goals were to read, write and think my way into questions I loved. Now I spend much of my day as a university administrator, where the quality of my work is measured in metrics and met deadlines. Somewhere along the way, my goals stopped being things I wanted and became things to check off.</p>

<p>Today’s productivity culture chases tops of its own, but it looks less like Kafka’s philosopher than like Lucy and Ethel working at the chocolate factory in the 1952 “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0043208/">I Love Lucy</a>” episode “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K3axU2b0dDk&amp;t">Job Switching</a>.” As the conveyor belt speeds up, the only way they can look like they’re keeping up is to stuff what they’ve missed into their mouths.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/K3axU2b0dDk?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Always trying to keep pace can often make you feel as if you’re a step behind.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Few things capture this pressure more than the SMART goal. In 1981, management consultant George Doran proposed that goals be <a href="https://openurl.ebsco.com/EPDB%3Agcd%3A2%3A40017010/detailv2?sid=ebsco%3Aocu%3Arecord&amp;id=ebsco%3Agcd%3A6043491&amp;bquery=IS%200025-1895%20AND%20VI%2070%20AND%20IP%2011%20AND%20DT%201981&amp;page=1&amp;link_origin=www.google.com&amp;searchDescription=Management%20Review%2C%201981%2C%20Vol%2070%2C%20Issue%2011&amp;crl=f">SMART</a>: specific, measurable, assignable, realistic and time-related. The <a href="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14649077">acronym spread</a> through industries and disciplines as a model for strategic planning, project management, performance evaluations and personal goal-setting. It distills a wider creed: Set the target, sprint after it,  hit it. Grasp the top, toss it, capture the next one, ad infinitum. Doran didn’t invent the impulse, but his acronym gave it a checklist. </p>

<p>Carson’s account of desire helps explain why this creed leads to two kinds of emptiness. </p>

<p>The first comes from pursuing goals people never really desired. <a href="https://marriott.byu.edu/magazine/feature/inbox-zero">Inbox zero</a> and a quarterly metric are goals in service of goals, the ultimate of which is productivity itself, which often simply ends up boosting someone else’s productivity.</p>

<p>The second comes from goals people truly wanted. Psychologist Tal Ben-Shahar calls the letdown that follows the “<a href="https://www.talbenshahar.com/media-podcasts-interviews-books-and/131d9eb6-fa14-48cd-9a2c-17a80f6884e3">arrival fallacy</a>” – the belief that reaching a destination will bring lasting happiness.  </p>

<p>The Greeks offer another kind of striving, one that locates pleasure in the pursuit itself rather than in the prize. In Plato’s “<a href="https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/1636/pg1636-images.html">Phaedrus</a>,” Socrates describes eros as giving the soul wings and treats philosophy as a love of wisdom no one can own. </p>

<p>Centuries later, philosopher <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/02/books/alasdair-macintyre-dead.html">Alasdair MacIntyre</a> distinguished external goods, such as money and status, from goods internal to a practice, such as a farmer’s growing mastery of her land or an architect’s pursuit of elegant, functional design. MacIntyre’s example, in his 1981 book “<a href="https://undpress.nd.edu/9780268035044/after-virtue/">After Virtue</a>,” is a child paid in candy to learn chess. As long as she plays for the candy, she has every reason to cheat. Only when she comes to love the game does she gain what chess itself can give: a particular kind of analytical skill, strategic imagination and competitive intensity.</p>

<p>To Socrates, MacIntyre and Carson, external goods get used up as they are won. Internal goods deepen the longer we pursue them.</p>

<p>Keeping desire alive means choosing pursuits that can never be finished – a craft, a field of study, a relationship – and letting the gap between reaching and grasping stay open. In this way, the lack that can hollow us out can also be what moves us. </p>

<p>Carson was handed the highest prize in literature. Yet the picture the Swedish Academy left us with is of a writer standing in the Icelandic wind, attending to a force of nature that no one can catch.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294825/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Florida Department of Health considers dropping 4 school vaccine requirements – here’s what that could mean for kids</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768516/original/file-20261027-52-9u04s1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C56%2C7119%2C4746&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Florida&#39;s Department of Health is considering ending the school requirement for vaccines against chickenpox.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/mommy-taking-care-of-her-ill-boy-royalty-free-image/1760667281?adppopup=true">ArtistGNDphotography/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The Florida Department of Health <a href="https://www.floridahealth.gov/2026/10/08/florida-department-of-health-holds-public-hearing-on-proposed-revisions-to-school-immunization-rule/">held a hearing</a> in October 2026 on a proposal to remove four vaccine requirements for entry into school and childcare: <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/23106-haemophilus-influenzae">Haemophilus influenzae type b, or Hib</a>, <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/4017-chickenpox">chickenpox</a>, <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/pneumococcal/index.html">pneumococcal</a> and <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/hepatitis-b/symptoms-causes/syc-20366802">hepatitis B</a>.</p>

<p>These vaccines entered use in the U.S. at different times from the early 1980s through 2000. Prior to that, there were millions of <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/chickenpox/vaccination-impact/index.html">chickenpox cases</a> and thousands of <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/pinkbook/hcp/table-of-contents/chapter-8-haemophilus-influenzae.html">serious bacterial infections</a> and preventable deaths among American children each year. Vaccination has <a href="https://theconversation.com/boost-your-immune-system-with-this-centuries-old-health-hack-vaccines-228567">dramatically reduced the toll</a> of these diseases.</p>

<p>Many parents today grew up during the transition to widespread vaccination for these diseases and may never have witnessed the severe complications these vaccines help prevent. I’m an <a href="https://publichealth.uic.edu/profiles/wallace-katrine/">epidemiologist</a> who studies <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=B5DbbcgAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">vaccine-preventable illnesses and health communication</a>, and I worry that perhaps the luxury of forgetting about these diseases could end up giving rise to a generation of children who aren’t vaccinated against them.</p>

<h2>What Florida would be choosing</h2>

<p>School vaccination requirements help communities establish <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/22599-herd-immunity">herd immunity</a>, which is when enough people are vaccinated to prevent a disease from easily spreading. When vaccination rates fall, infections can spread among susceptible children throughout the community, placing those who are too young to be fully vaccinated, as well as those who cannot develop adequate protection due to medical conditions, at greater risk.</p>

<p>Florida’s proposal would not eliminate these four vaccines, nor would ending a mandate mean that every family would stop using them. However, it would weaken one of the policies designed to maintain high vaccination coverage. If fewer children are vaccinated as a result, the risks will <a href="https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/193407">extend beyond</a> the families making that choice. </p>

<p>The consequences could be devastating.</p>

<h2>Hib: The bacterium that can cause meningitis</h2>

<p>Before Hib vaccines became widely used in the late 1980s, pediatricians sometimes faced a terrifying emergency: an infant with fever, lethargy and a stiff neck. Testing of cerebrospinal fluid would reveal bacterial meningitis caused by <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/23106-haemophilus-influenzae">Haemophilus influenzae type b, or Hib</a>, an infection that could kill a child or leave lasting neurological damage.</p>

<p>Today, many doctors have never even seen a single case. The bacterium has not disappeared, but widespread vaccination has made serious Hib disease in young children far less common.</p>

<p>Before the vaccine, Hib was the <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/pinkbook/hcp/table-of-contents/chapter-8-haemophilus-influenzae.html">leading cause of bacterial meningitis</a>. In the early 1980s, there were <a href="https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/media/pressrel/r981127.htm">20,000 invasive Hib infections</a> among American children under 5 years old, 12,000 of which were meningitis. <a href="https://www.immunize.org/ask-experts/how-common-is-haemophilus-influenzae-type-b-hib-disease/">Between 3% and 6% of those children died</a>, and between 15% and 30% of the survivors were left deaf or with brain damage. </p>

<p>Hib infection did not manifest in dramatic outbreaks. Healthy young children carried it silently, and some, unpredictably, became seriously ill.</p>

<p>After the introduction of <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements/haemophilus-b-conjugate-vaccine-intramuscular-route/description/drg-20069853">conjugate vaccines for Hib</a> in the late 1980s, cases among young children <a href="https://www.immunize.org/ask-experts/how-common-is-haemophilus-influenzae-type-b-hib-disease/">declined by 99%</a>. In 2023, the United States reported <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/hi-disease/media/pdfs/2025/07/HiPSS2023_FINAL_508c.pdf">only 13 cases in children under 5</a>. In 2026, that number is <a href="https://data.cdc.gov/NNDSS/NNDSS-Weekly-Data/x9gk-5huc/data_preview">up to 28</a>.</p>

<h2>Chickenpox: The ‘harmless’ rite of passage</h2>

<p>By the early 1990s, there were <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html">more than 4 million cases</a> of <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/4017-chickenpox">chickenpox</a> annually in the United States. Of those infected, 10,500 to 13,500 were hospitalized, and 100 to 150 died. More than 90% of cases and about 70% of hospitalizations occurred in children, as did roughly half of the deaths. </p>

<p>But even those who had manageable cases of childhood chickenpox are <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/shingles/symptoms-causes/syc-20353054">at risk for shingles</a> later in life, which can lead to <a href="https://theconversation.com/shingles-can-cause-severe-chronic-pain-new-research-on-how-exosomes-alter-neurons-offers-pathways-to-treatment-290398">painful and sometimes permanent health complications</a>.</p>

<p>Children are contagious before the rash appears, and each case has an incubation period of <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/chickenpox/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html">up to three weeks</a>. A single infection could spread through a school or daycare in waves for a month or more. Since vaccination began in 1995, deaths from chickenpox in people under 20 years old have been <a href="https://www.healio.com/news/infectious-disease/20221020/varicella-deaths-in-us-have-practically-been-eliminated-by-vaccination">virtually eliminated</a>.</p>

            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768524/original/file-20261027-52-rqjld0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="woman with glasses using otoscope to look into child's ear" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768524/original/file-20261027-52-rqjld0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768524/original/file-20261027-52-rqjld0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768524/original/file-20261027-52-rqjld0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768524/original/file-20261027-52-rqjld0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768524/original/file-20261027-52-rqjld0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768524/original/file-20261027-52-rqjld0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768524/original/file-20261027-52-rqjld0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Pneumococcus: Serious infections</h2>

<p><a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/24231-pneumococcal-disease">Pneumococcal bacteria</a> can live harmlessly in a child’s <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/24231-pneumococcal-disease">upper respiratory tract – that is, the nose</a> – but if it moves into the blood or organs, it can cause serious damage.</p>

<p>Before the introduction of the childhood vaccine in 2000, pneumococcal disease caused <a href="https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2001/0515/p1991.html">about 17,000</a> invasive infections annually in American children under 5 years old, including about <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00033405.htm">700 cases of meningitis and 200 deaths</a>. On top of that, pneumococcal disease caused approximately 5 million ear infections.</p>

<h2>Hepatitis B: The silent threat</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/hepatitis-b/symptoms-causes/syc-20366802">Hepatitis B</a> can spread from an infected mother to her baby during childbirth and through contact with infected blood. People with chronic hepatitis B may have no symptoms and may not know they are infected, allowing the virus to spread unknowingly within families and communities. Infected infants and young children also are often asymptomatic.</p>

<p>Yet the consequences can be serious. Infants who become infected with hepatitis B have about a <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/hepatitis-b/hcp/clinical-overview/">90% chance of developing chronic hepatitis B</a>, which over time can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer. The risk of chronic infection falls sharply with age, making prevention of infection early in life particularly important.</p>

<p>Before the hepatitis B vaccine became available in the U.S. in 1982, <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00033405.htm">an estimated 20,000 American children</a> were infected each year. </p>

<p>In 1991, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommended universal infant hepatitis B vaccination as part of a comprehensive strategy to prevent transmission. The CDC estimates that perinatal hepatitis B infections in the United States <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5125a3.htm">declined by 75%</a> between 1987 and 2000.</p>

<h2>Florida’s future</h2>

<p>Florida’s historical records for these diseases are incomplete. For example, chickenpox was not a disease tracked by the Florida Department of Health <a href="https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/16/4/09-0688_article">until late 2006</a>. That makes it difficult to reconstruct the state’s prevaccine impact of these diseases from surveillance records alone.</p>

<p>But Florida doesn’t have to imagine what happens when vaccination is neglected: Measles has resurfaced in the state this year. It had previously been <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/about/history.html">eliminated nationally in 2000</a>, meaning sustained endemic transmission had been interrupted. The disease has never been eradicated globally, and imported infections can trigger outbreaks when they reach undervaccinated communities.</p>

<p>An outbreak at Ave Maria University outside of Naples infected <a href="https://www.wuwf.org/florida-news/2026-05-18/no-measles-cases-in-florida-over-most-recent-week-of-reporting">at least 62 people</a>, and the state reported <a href="https://www.flhealthcharts.gov/ChartsReports/rdPage.aspx?rdReport=FrequencyMerlin.Frequency&amp;FirstTime=True">162 cases</a> as of Oct. 17, 2026. This is the most recent available data at the time of this article’s publication.</p>

<p>The proposal to stop requiring vaccines for hepatitis B, chickenpox, Hib and pneumococcal comes as <a href="https://www.flhealthcharts.gov/ChartsDashboards/rdPage.aspx?rdReport=NonVitalIndNoGrp.Dataviewer&amp;cid=75">only 88.9% of Florida kindergartners</a> received the <a href="https://www.stanfordchildrens.org/en/topic/default?id=measles-mumps-and-rubella-mmr-vaccine-90-P02250">measles, mumps, rubella – or MMR</a> – vaccine during the 2025-26 school year. This is below both the U.S. <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/schoolvaxview/data/index.html">national average of 92.4%</a> and the recommended <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/global-measles-vaccination/about/index.html">threshold of 95%</a> to create herd immunity.</p>

<p>Unfortunately, it’s been difficult to know current measles rates in Florida. In May 2026, the Florida Department of Health <a href="https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida/2025/05/09/florida-disease-database-county-data-not-available">removed county-level disease data</a> from its website. The data has since been replaced, but there is currently no measles dashboard to track cases in the state. The department’s 2026 counts have <a href="https://www.wusf.org/health-news-florida/2026-02-09/measles-spreading-florida-state-updates-lag-more-than-week">often been delayed</a>, and <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html">public tracking systems disagree</a> on the statewide total.</p>

<p>An entire generation of parents has been spared the experience of seeing a child with Hib meningitis, or young adults with liver problems from chronic hepatitis B. Nor have they had to deal with finding alternate childcare for a month because a chickenpox outbreak has shut down their child’s preschool. These are achievements of vaccination – and a reminder of what can be forgotten when prevention works.</p>

body: Florida's Department of Health is considering ending the school requirement for vaccines against chickenpox

ArtistGNDphotography/E+ via Getty Images The Florida Department of Health held a hearing in October 2026 on a proposal to remove four vaccine requirements for entry into school and childcare: Haemophilus influenzae type b, or Hib , chickenpox , pneumococcal and hepatitis B
These vaccines entered use in the U.S. at different times from the early 1980s through 2000
Prior to that, there were millions of chickenpox cases and thousands of serious bacterial infections and preventable deaths among American children each year
Vaccination has dramatically reduced the toll of these diseases
Many parents today grew up during the transition to widespread vaccination for these diseases and may never have witnessed the severe complications these vaccines help prevent

I’m an epidemiologist who studies vaccine-preventable illnesses and health communication , and I worry that perhaps the luxury of forgetting about these diseases could end up giving rise to a generation of children who aren’t vaccinated against them
What Florida would be choosing School vaccination requirements help communities establish herd immunity , which is when enough people are vaccinated to prevent a disease from easily spreading

When vaccination rates fall, infections can spread among susceptible children throughout the community, placing those who are too young to be fully vaccinated, as well as those who cannot develop adequate protection due to medical conditions, at greater risk
Florida’s proposal would not eliminate these four vaccines, nor would ending a mandate mean that every family would stop using them
However, it would weaken one of the policies designed to maintain high vaccination coverage
If fewer children are vaccinated as a result, the risks will extend beyond the families making that choice

Hib: The bacterium that can cause meningitis Before Hib vaccines became widely used in the late 1980s, pediatricians sometimes faced a terrifying emergency: an infant with fever, lethargy and a stiff neck
Testing of cerebrospinal fluid would reveal bacterial meningitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b, or Hib , an infection that could kill a child or leave lasting neurological damage
Today, many doctors have never even seen a single case
The bacterium has not disappeared, but widespread vaccination has made serious Hib disease in young children far less common
Before the vaccine, Hib was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis
In the early 1980s, there were 20,000 invasive Hib infections among American children under 5 years old, 12,000 of which were meningitis
Between 3% and 6% of those children died , and between 15% and 30% of the survivors were left deaf or with brain damage
Hib infection did not manifest in dramatic outbreaks
Healthy young children carried it silently, and some, unpredictably, became seriously ill
After the introduction of conjugate vaccines for Hib in the late 1980s, cases among young children declined by 99%
In 2023, the United States reported only 13 cases in children under 5
Chickenpox: The ‘harmless’ rite of passage By the early 1990s, there were more than 4 million cases of chickenpox annually in the United States
Of those infected, 10,500 to 13,500 were hospitalized, and 100 to 150 died
More than 90% of cases and about 70% of hospitalizations occurred in children, as did roughly half of the deaths
But even those who had manageable cases of childhood chickenpox are at risk for shingles later in life, which can lead to painful and sometimes permanent health complications
Children are contagious before the rash appears, and each case has an incubation period of up to three weeks
A single infection could spread through a school or daycare in waves for a month or more
Since vaccination began in 1995, deaths from chickenpox in people under 20 years old have been virtually eliminated
Middle ear infections are more common among children who have not been vaccinated against pneumococcal disease

Jose Luis Pelaez Inc/DigitalVision via Getty Images Pneumococcus: Serious infections Pneumococcal bacteria can live harmlessly in a child’s upper respiratory tract – that is, the nose – but if it moves into the blood or organs, it can cause serious damage

Before the introduction of the childhood vaccine in 2000, pneumococcal disease caused about 17,000 invasive infections annually in American children under 5 years old, including about 700 cases of meningitis and 200 deaths
On top of that, pneumococcal disease caused approximately 5 million ear infections
Hepatitis B: The silent threat Hepatitis B can spread from an infected mother to her baby during childbirth and through contact with infected blood
People with chronic hepatitis B may have no symptoms and may not know they are infected, allowing the virus to spread unknowingly within families and communities
Infected infants and young children also are often asymptomatic

title: Is this our last time setting our clocks back?
excerpt: This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscri
body: This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
Hi readers, happy Friday! We have a big weekend coming up: Halloween, the New York Marathon — and the end of daylight saving time
At 2 am on Sunday, our clocks will fall back one hour, returning us to standard time for the next four and a half months or so

Depending on who you ask, it’s either the welcome return of before-work sunshine, or the start of a dreary slog through 4:30 pm sunsets. (The good news, though, is that however you feel about falling back, it’s  not nearly as hard on the body as springing forward will be in March, when we return to daylight saving time.) It’s also a topic that draws strong opinions, including in the pages of Vox (which has both pointed out the awfulness of daylight saving time and argued that it should go on forever ).  President Donald Trump, of all people, is a strong proponent of the latter view: Several times this month, he’s harangued the US Senate to pass a bill making daylight saving time — that is, the time we’re in from March to early November, with later sunrises and later sunsets — permanent year-round, even posting the personal cellphone number of permanent DST opponent Sen
Tom Cotton (R-AR).  Despite his lobbying, the Senate hasn’t taken action
But should it? Is there a better solution, or are we best off the way things are, despite the burrs? We get into that and more below

Time for the daylight saving time debate View Link As we mentioned above, a bill to establish permanent daylight saving time — the Sunshine Protection Act — is currently on hold in the Senate after passing the House by an overwhelming margin this summer

Nineteen US states have also passed laws that would do the same thing, though they won’t be able to take effect until or unless Congress acts, too. (Two US states, Arizona and Hawaii, are currently on permanent standard time, which is allowed.) Advocates say that more daylight in the evening gives Americans more time to pursue leisure activities after work (the golf industry is a big fan ), plus it may even have some positive effect on crime rates and the economy.  But the utopian ideal of no more darkness before 5 pm may not be all that it’s cracked up to be
Critics of the permanent time change point out that the US has tried permanent DST before, and it was not well received

As the Washingtonian reported in 2022, “While 79 percent of Americans approved of the change in December 1973, approval had  dropped to 42 percent three months later.”  That’s because there’s still only so much sunlight to go around, and permanent DST makes for very dark winter mornings — think sunrises after 9 am along the western edges of time zones

When it took effect in the ’70s, it quickly  proved dangerous for children heading to school in the dark.  As Vox reported in 2016, courtesy of the cartographer Andy Woodruff, the change would leave most people with a  markedly worse sunrise situation in exchange for an after-work boost

If we still want to escape the biannual time change, though, the opposite solution might be preferable: Permanent standard time leaves more people with a reasonable sunrise time, and has  less of an impact on what people described as a reasonable sunset time (really — check out the maps in the story here )

It’s also considered the healthiest option by the  American Academy of Sleep Medicine , which notes that permanent standard time better aligns with our circadian rhythms.  The most likely option, though, is that we keep muddling along like this: Darker evenings are a hard political sell, and Congress abandoned its last permanent DST experiment after less than a year
At least we mostly won’t have to reset our clocks manually on Sunday morning
One link for later ➨ How to do Halloween in a hurry

If you’re short on time and/or money and still in need of a Halloween costume, my colleague Allie Volpe has some advice on ways to tap your creativity (and closet) to pull something off at the last minute

Before you go… Did you know… that some right-wingers, including Vice President JD Vance, are trying to rehabilitate the reputation of President Richard Nixon , who resigned in disgrace after the Watergate scandal and his attempts at a cover-up came to light?  Today’s trivia: Who is the reclusive neighbor to the Finch family in the classic novel To Kill a Mockingbird ? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in Monday’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday, we asked about the name of the vast Andean empire that ruled from its capital in Cusco
That would be the Inca Empire, which covered much of western South America in the 15th and 16th centuries.

title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
excerpt: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test
body: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test
They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded
Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website
It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI
In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track

And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.  AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts
That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time

But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.  Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes
That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine , we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences.  And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability : the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems
In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it
And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely
Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not

They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions
So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks
This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important
With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit
We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures
Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks
This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.  The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed
Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions

The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken
Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans
The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision
In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took

And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from
Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible

The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it
OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized
The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory
And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people
Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging

The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used

No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.  AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory

Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist
Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules
Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry

We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.  No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong
Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this
And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable

title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
excerpt: A dangerous blind spot in climate models: Current models used to inform major UN climate reports fail to account for powerful feedback loops—where warming itsel
body: A dangerous blind spot in climate models: Current models used to inform major UN climate reports fail to account for powerful feedback loops—where warming itself drives more warming—leaving us underestimating how fast temperatures could rise
The numbers are alarming: Thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, warming wetlands and other feedbck effects could add 0.2°C to 0.4°C of extra warming this century

Scientists are scrambling to catch up: Over 20 international research teams are now running coordinated analyses to better understand these feedback effects, with hopes the UN will incorporate findings into its next major climate assessment in 2029. " data-chronoton-post-id="1147735" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change

Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be
And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century

A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs , and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century
That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100

The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding.  None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects

That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries

A separate analysis published in One Earth in March , which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed

It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds
Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects

Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.  At least some of this is starting to happen

Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project , through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power
Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029
That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds
But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution

And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.  So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control

Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story )

In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.  Several startups are also exploring possibilities

They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control
Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile

But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.  The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.  This article is from The Spark,  MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter

title: Creating AI value with enterprise context
excerpt: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assis
body: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools
Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond
But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business
Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments

DOWNLOAD THE REPORT An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments

The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all
Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%)

Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes. “There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here
It’s just not really useful in most companies today.” The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business
A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms)

It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says
